en: Having exerted great effort in the *Mahābhāṣya* of Patañjali, the wise [Nāgeśa], son of Śivabhaṭṭa and born from the womb of Satīdevī, [composed this work]. (1)
Having obtained his livelihood from Rāma, the sovereign of Śṛṅgaverapura, who was a wish-fulfilling tree for supplicants and a fire for the thicket of his enemies. || 2 ||
Having bowed to the Lord of Serpents, Nāgeśa composes the *Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara*, which illuminates the meaning and possesses the beautiful Umā as half of his body.

Performing an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) in the form of a salutation to the three sages (*munitraya*) for the sake of pacifying the evil (*durita*) that obstructs the completion of the work and its dissemination, the author composes this verse—beginning with "The three sages"—for the instruction of his disciples, and incidentally for the auspiciousness of the commentator and the audience. The accusative case is used because it possesses greater force than other case-terminations. Regarding the word *paribhāvya*: since the pronoun *tat* refers to what is present in the mind, the meaning is "having set aside the statements of the ancients," or alternatively, "having reflected upon the statements of the three sages."

Since the lexicon states that "paribhāva means contempt," there is no contradiction in the root *bhū*—which normally signifies contempt—having the sense of "investigation" (vicāra) here, because roots possess multiple meanings. For this very reason, the rule "with the prefix *pari*, the root *bhū* is used in the sense of contempt" is consistent. By this, it is implied that his own work does not merely repeat what is found in ancient texts and that it possesses a firm foundation. Furthermore, the designation "this [work]" (*iyam*) is used because even future things can be made objects of the intellect.

Its similarity to moonlight lies in its illuminating the established tenets (*siddhānta*) and in its capacity to alleviate the distressing heat that arises when seeking knowledge of those tenets from other extremely difficult texts. By this, it is indicated that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) consists of the grammatical tenets, the purpose (*prayojana*) is the knowledge thereof, and the qualified student (*adhikārī*) is one who desires to know them, and so forth.

Although *aiuṇ* indicates their sequence, it is a technical definition (*saṃjñāsūtra*) because, through syntactic unity with the rule "the first [vowel] with the last," it delimits the scope of the grammatical operation (*vṛtti*). This is because the sequence is useful only by means of the technical definitions. This syntactic unity is as follows: the first vowel, beginning with *a*, when uttered together with the last one, beginning with *ṇ*, which is similar to it, serves as the technical name for those vowels implied by the first and last. It should be understood that rules such as *svaujas* are also technical definitions of case-endings (*sub*) and so forth, and serve to prescribe the suffixes *su* and others, precisely because they share this same syntactic unity. In these cases, the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is not intended to be expressed.

There is no application of the rules for *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination). Furthermore, because it is a quotation (*anukaraṇa*) and is treated as a *sūtra*-like form, case-endings (*vibhakti*) do not arise after the phonemes. Nor does the suffix *kāra* apply, due to the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*). As for the claim that "no euphonic combination (*sandhi*) occurs because it would contradict what has been relied upon": for instance, at the time when the technical names (*saṃjñā*) such as *ac* and so on are being grasped, rules such as *ād guṇaḥ* have not yet come into effect because they are not yet established; thus, the word-potency (*pada-śakti*) for terms like *ac* is grasped with respect to the unmodified forms *a*, *ā*, etc. Later, once the pratyāhāra *ac* is known, if those [rules] were to apply here—as they do in the case of *upendra*—it would lead to a contradiction. This is because, once a *sandhi*-operation has been performed, the original unmodified form is no longer heard.

That is not so; for since no other meaning has been apprehended for the word *ac*, there is no contradiction with that [meaning]. Nor is there doubt regarding the *saṃhitā* [reading], because a definitive determination is possible through the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

Now, an objection might be raised: since the terms *āmnāya* and *samāmnāya* are well-known in common usage only for the Veda, the designation "the collection of phonemes" (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) for the fourteen-sūtra text is untenable. To this he says: "The Maheśvaras. This means they have come from Maheśvara; the implication is that they were obtained through the grace of Maheśvara. Thus, this is indeed a Śruti (revelation) with such a specific sequence, which was received by Pāṇini through his grace. Because it is rooted in Śruti, it alone possesses the status of a Vedic auxiliary (*vedāṅga*). The proof is the statement in the Śikṣā: "Having received the collection of phonemes from Maheśvara, [Pāṇini] proclaimed the entire Grammar."

In passages such as "The activity of the Teacher regarding the letter *ṇ* in the *laṇ*-sūtra makes known [the principle] that [the meaning of a rule] is determined through exposition (*vyākhyānataḥ*)," the term "Teacher" (*ācārya*) refers to Maheśvara. Furthermore, the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) possess meaning like Maheśvara; they are not at all meaningless. Thus is their purpose. Regarding the statement in the *vṛddhi*-sūtra, "A phoneme cannot be meaningless," this refers to the absence of a communicable meaning (*bodhyārtha*). It does not mean that the phoneme is useless in its own form (*svarūpa*); otherwise, the Bhāṣya’s subsequent explanations—which appear to reject [the necessity of certain *anubandhas*]—would be inconsistent.

For this very reason, taking up the *Bhāṣya* which states, "This collection of phonemes (*akṣara-samāmnāya*) is like a flowering and fruiting tree, adorned like the moon and the stars—a mass of Brahman," Bhartṛhari has said:

"Just as this [world] consisting of the moon, stars, and so forth is uninterrupted, even so there is no modern author of this collection of phonemes; it is remembered exactly thus through the tradition of the Vedas. Here, "modern" refers to one who possesses a body. Its "flowering" occurs by means of the science of grammar (*śabda-śāstra*) rooted therein, and its "fruiting" occurs through the actual employment of words.
And this has been stated in the *Kāśikā* composed by Nandikeśvara as a commentary on the fourteen aphorisms (*sūtra*):
"At the conclusion of the dance, the King of Dancers sounded his drum nine and five times,
desiring to uplift the perfected ones such as Sanaka and others regarding this web of Śiva’s aphorisms through this inquiry."
"In all these sūtras, the final fourteenth letter is taught as the *dhātu-artha* (the meaning of the verbal root) for the sake of accomplishing what is desired by Pāṇini and others.

Here, *dhātvartham* means for the purpose of the operation of the science of grammar which is rooted in the verbal roots (*dhātu*). For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The instruction of the letters is for the purpose of [attaching] the *anubandhas*. By the use of the word *karaṇa* (purpose/means) here, the fact that the *anubandhas* have a beginning (*sāditva*) is indicated. And since that purpose belongs to the agent who performs the instruction, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is thereby indicated that everything else apart from that [instruction] is beginningless (*anāditva*).

In this context, by the desire to uplift Sanaka and others, its nature as an instruction from Brahmā is indicated; and that [nature] is not consistent with the absence of being a Śruti (Vedic revelation), because of the statement: "It is to be heard from the sentences of the Śruti."

In the *Ṛktantravyākaraṇa*, Śākaṭāyana also states: "This syllabic meter (*akṣarachandas*) has been set forth according to its phonemes (*varṇaśas*), just as the Teachers have said: 'Brahmā spoke it to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati to Indra; Indra to Bharadvāja; Bharadvāja to the seers (*ṛṣis*); and the seers to the Brahmins. They indeed call this the traditional collection of syllables (*akṣarasamāmnāya*). One should not recite this mass of sacred knowledge (*brahmarāśi*) after eating, nor at night. The meaning of "mass of sacred knowledge" (*brahmarāśi*) is "the collection of phonemes that expounds Brahman. This point is made clear in the *Kāśikā* composed by Nandikeśvara.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The instruction of the phonemes (varṇas) must be performed for the purpose of their coalescence in grammatical operations (vṛtti-samavāya). The meaning of this is that it is for the sake of that coalescence—the sequential arrangement of the phonemes—which results in the efficient application of Pāṇini’s rules through brevity (lāghava). And this [coalescence] serves the purpose of applying the rules by means of pratyāhāras such as *aṇ* and others. Thus, it is clearly stated that this instruction was composed by someone other than Pāṇini.

The use of the word *upadeśa* here is similar to its use in the phrase *mantropadeśa*. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the fruit of knowing this [grammar] is the merit arising from the complete study (*pārāyaṇa*) of all the Vedas. Furthermore, the Chāndogya Śruti, beginning with "the grammar of the Vedas" (*vedānāṃ vedaḥ*), has precisely this as its purport; such is the direction of the argument. He states its purpose: "for the sake of technical names" (*saṃjñārthāni*). This has already been established. It should be understood that the introduction of technical names is for the sake of the efficient operation of the treatise through brevity (*lāghava*). To justify their being for the sake of technical names, he says: "of these" (*eṣām*).

"And the letter *a*. By this, the formation of the *raprattyāhāra* (the abbreviation *ra*) is established. It is mentioned separately because it is not final [in the alphabet]. This is in accordance with Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra "Tulyāsyaprayatnam" (Pāṇini 1.1.9). Others, however, argue that if this [letter *a*] were nasal (*anunāsika*), Pāṇini would not have pronounced the letter *l* in the sūtra "ato lrān" (Pāṇini 7.2.73), since the purpose could have been served by the *prattyāhāra* alone. Furthermore, if this [letter *a*] possessed the technical designation *it*, he would have employed the *yaprattyāhāra* instead in many sūtras containing the word *yaṇ*, for the sake of the brevity of half a *mātrā*.

Furthermore, if the *an* group were not included in the *ac* pratyāhāra, there would be the undesirable consequence that the third reason stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, "because of usage, because it is subordinate, and because elision (*lopa*) is more powerful"—would be non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). This is because, even if elision were powerful according to your view, the meaning of the term *ac* could not be established prior to the establishment of the *hal* pratyāhāra.

Since there is no rule in the *upadeśa* (the original instruction) stating "aja," and since the *it*-designation and subsequent elision of the vowel *a* in *laṇ* do not occur, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has established as his final conclusion that in the formation of *pratyāhāras*, only the view of grasping the genus (*jāti*) is valid. Consequently, if the vowel *a* were included in the *laṇ* *pratyāhāra*, then in the word *māmām̐strāyasva*, the occurrence of an *anusvāra* would be unavoidable under the alternative where the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel is accepted; furthermore, in forms such as *so'sti*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the case-ending *su*. For this very reason, it is said:
"How is it that in the *pratyāhāras*, the *anubandhas* [are not included] when there is the mention of *ac*?"

By this [statement], a doubt has been raised regarding the *ac* pratyāhāra—meaning "why is there no inclusion by the mention of *ac* of those *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) which are made as pratyāhāras within the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the traditional list of phonemes) in the sūtras that indicate *ac*?"—but not regarding the *hat* pratyāhāra. Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya, its application is shown precisely through the citation of the four sūtras beginning with "aiuṇ."

In this regard, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that among the *pratyāhāras*, the primary status consists in their being for the purpose of inclusion (*grahaṇārthatva*); and while the consonants (*hal*) are taught in that manner, it is specifically the vowels (*svara*) that are taught as such among the *akṣaras*. Therefore, due to their predominance, they alone possess the status of the named (*saṃjñitva*). Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of including the letter *ṭ* in the *pratyāhāra* *haś* and others; for since the vowel *a* is pronounced repeatedly after the consonants beginning with *ha*, it can be maintained that consonants devoid of phonemes intended merely for pronunciation are not included in a *pratyāhāra* composed of them.

Furthermore, because there is no mention of applications [of the rule] regarding that [subject], its nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) is therefore without authoritative basis. They say that in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, the mention of *l* must indeed be made, just as there is a mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the sounds *ṛ* and *l*.

One might object: "In cases such as *'haya'* and so forth, by the pronunciation of the vowel *a*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that [consonant *h*] being classified as a *hal* (consonant). To this he replies: "In the case of *hakāra* and so forth. The sense is that this is based on the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *uccair udāttaḥ*, which states: "Furthermore, the utterance of a consonant (*vyañjana*) does not occur without a vowel," and also on the *Bhāṣya* on the rule regarding the *anubandhas* in the *pratyāhāra*: "For this style of the Teacher is observed, that he teaches those of the same class among those of the same class—vowels among vowels and consonants among consonants."

It might be argued as follows: For the sake of making rules such as *na vibhaktau* meaningful, it is necessary that *halantyam* mean "the final consonant (*hal*) in an *upadeśa* is an *it*. Since the rules *halantyam* and *ādirantyena* are mutually dependent, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, it would be improper for Pāṇini to teach the *it*-designation for the consonants (*hal*) without first teaching the *it*-designation for the letter *l*. Nor can it be said that by repeating the sequence starting with *hayavaraṭ*, one should enjoin the *hal*-designation for the entire collection ending with *śaṣasar* by means of the term *hal*; for this would involve the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of repeating ten sūtras.

Now, one might object: let there be three sūtras—‘upadeśe 'jantyam’, ‘ac’, and ‘anunāsikaḥ’. Here, ‘ac’ is for the purpose of excluding non-vowels (anantyārtha). In the third sūtra, by the force of the continued application (anuvṛtti) of ‘ac’, a restriction (niyama) is adopted: if it is a vowel (ac) that becomes short (it), then it must be nasalized (anunāsika). Thus, there is no fault in the case of *rup* and so on. Furthermore, by the force of the division of the rule (yogavibhāga), this restriction applies even to what is separated [from the preceding], overriding the maxim ‘the operation applies to what is immediately adjacent’ (*anantarasya*).

Moreover, because of the indicator (jñāpaka) in the rule ‘midaco 'ntyāt’, there is no reverse restriction (viparītaniyama). And in this way, the mention of ‘hal’ is also redundant, and the charge of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) does not arise.

Nor should it be said that there is a loss of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit) in the recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) and so forth when there is a variation in Pāṇini’s rules, for the *Bhāṣya* states in various places: "But it becomes non-Pāṇinian. This is not a fault provided the newly proposed formulation (*nyāsa*) is more concise. Regarding the variation of a rule (*sūtrabheda*), they apply that term only where a different rule is created, or where the same rule is restated in greater detail; this is established by the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* and its *Bhāṣya*. The phrase "this is not a variation of a rule" implies that it does not constitute a fault.

His intention is that, when possible, the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) have only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) by way of being directly perceived (*dṛṣṭadvāra*). Therefore, if it is argued that there is no annihilation of the entire Bhāṣya which provides evidence for this here and there, we say no; for there would be excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) in resorting to the assumption of rules regarding word-division (*yogavibhāga*) and indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*). There is certainly no royal decree stating that one should respect only the complexity of the physical impact of the throat and other organs that produces the manifestation of phonemes (*varṇābhivyakti*), but not the complexity of the mental operation that generates knowledge.

Furthermore, one should not argue that the term *sahetā* means "the middle class of letters" (i.e., the vowels) because they come (*eti*) together with (*saha*) the prefix *ā* on all sides (*samantāt*); for the Commentator, when he speaks of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and its avoidance, demonstrates in the case of *kaṭī vī* that the suffix *tṛc* does not occur after the root *īṅ* (meaning "to go") preceded by *sa-* and *ā-*. Moreover, according to the rules of grammatical derivation (*yogamaryādā*), the aforementioned meaning cannot be obtained from that [interpretation]. Furthermore, the phrase *ā samantāt* would be either syntactically disconnected or redundant. Since there is no evidence for this being a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), he avoids that [objection] by repeating the sūtra: *halantyam*.

In the Bhāṣya as well, having raised the objection of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), it is stated: "It should be said that 'the final sound among the *hal* [consonants] has the designation *it*, provided that it is the sound *l*. Then it is said: "Or rather, it is established by means of an *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) reference: *hal* and *hal* are *hal*; thus, 'the final among the *hal*' is said. The meaning of this is as follows: through the word *hal*, which has undergone *ekaśeṣa*, there is a compound with the genitive of general relation (*sambandhasāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*); and the word *antya* (final), being heard at the end of the *dvandva*, is construed with both [members]. Thus, the understanding is: "the final among the *hal*s" and "that which is final in the form of a *hal*."

In the final case, the genitive case is used as in the expression "the head of Rāhu" (*arāhoḥ śiraḥ*). Here, for the speaker, there is a mention using *ekaśeṣa* (a single term representing multiple instances), whereas for the listener, comprehension occurs through repetition. Regarding Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, which states, "The *lakāra* near *it* [is] *it*, and that which is final among the *hal*s [is also *it*]," one should infer that he would have said: "A *hal* becomes marked with the technical designation *it*, provided it is the final among the *hal*s."

If it is objected: "Even so, the understanding of *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes—which are denoted by the word 'vibhakti' in the rule *na vibhaktau*—occurs only after the understanding of the meaning of the sentence *halantyam*; and that understanding [of *halantyam*] occurs only after the understanding of the meaning of the exception (*apavāda*) sentence [namely, *na vibhaktau*]. Thus, the circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) remains exactly as it was," we reply: No; because prior to the understanding of the meaning of the exception sentence, when the word and its meaning are presented, there is no obstacle to the understanding of the meaning of the general rule (*utsarga*).

For no one accepts that the cognition of an absence is a cause for the cognition of its counter-positive, in the same way that the cognition of a counter-positive is accepted as a cause for the cognition of an absence; moreover, it is because the meaning of a negative sentence is impossible without the cognition of the counter-positive.

The meaning of the statement, "For exceptions (*apavāda*) apply first, and general rules (*utsarga*) afterwards," is as follows: For one whose sole eye is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), when a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a general rule has arisen regarding everything delimited by the delimiter of the intended object (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), there would result an inability to establish the distinct domains of the general rule and the exception. Furthermore, this would lead to the redundancy of the exceptional rule, like the sentence "Do not eat" addressed to one who has already eaten. Therefore, by examining the exceptional rule, one determines the formation of the intended object (*lakṣya*) that falls within its domain, and [then applies the general rule] to that which is outside its domain.

It refines each respective object of denotation by opening the floodgate for the influence of its corresponding specific sentence-meaning; otherwise, there would be the contingency of optionality (*vikalpa*).

Although the maxim "with respect to one who has already eaten" is contradicted by cases where [an operation] that has arisen is removed through elision (*luk*) and so forth, even in those cases there is simply non-origination, and thus no fault arises; furthermore, this is because the contingency of optionality remains even if one does not accept that maxim. The meaning of the phrase "they enter into" (*abhiniviśante*) is that they become established in the intellect (*buddhi*).

However, one whose sole eye is the *lakṣya* (the actual linguistic usage) understands the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *lakṣya* through the general rule (*utsarga*), even without a detailed investigation of the various grammatical treatises (*śāstra*), provided he avoids the scope of exceptions (*apavāda*). For even such a person, merit (*dharma*) arises only from usage preceded by the recollection of the grammatical system (*śāstraprakriyā*). As it has been said: "Having set aside the scope of the exception, the general rule then operates. Here, "having set aside" (*prakalpya*) means having avoided (*parityajya*).

As for the claim that the meaning of the phrase "having postulated" (*prakalpya ca*) is as follows—namely, that according to the statement "when there is *samprasāraṇa*," the *samprasāraṇa* occurs first for the subsequent semivowel (*yaṇ*), while the prohibition caused by that [subsequent change] applies to the preceding one—as Kaiyaṭa states in the commentary on the rule defining the term *abhyasta*: that is not so, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "not when there is *samprasāraṇa*" (*na samprasāraṇe*). For in that *Bhāṣya*, it is stated: "This very [sūtra] indicates that [the prohibition] does not apply to the preceding [vowel], or rather, that there is a prohibition for that which depends upon *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth.

Indeed, such a statement is not appropriate when [the matter] is established by logic (*nyāya*). Therefore, it should be understood that the scope of logic is precisely what I have stated. Even if it is argued that "the meaning of a general rule (*utsarga*) cannot exist without the meaning of an exception (*apavāda*)," that too is not so, for the reason already stated. In the grammatical treatise, by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*, merely through knowing the referents of the words *tu* and *sm*, one understands—by realizing that the suffixes beginning with *p* do not fall within its scope—that the rule *halantyam* applies to them; thus, the knowledge of the referents of the word *vibhakti* (in the form of *sup* and *tiṅ*) becomes easily accessible. This is the direction of the argument.
The phrase "instruction" (upadeśa) is also connected here. He states the meaning obtainable by the force of that [instruction] with the words: "in the sūtra."

"By the first [letter] together with the last. Why is "the first" mentioned? Because the word "last" implies those that precede it, there might be an apprehension that in the *pratyāhāra* "ak" (beginning with *a*), the letter *a* and so forth would not be included. Similarly, because the word "first" implies those that follow it, there might be an apprehension that in the *pratyāhāras* beginning with "iṇ" and so on, letters such as *ña* and others would not be included. Therefore, the phrase "by the last" is used. However, when both "the first" and "with the last" are employed, there is no fault; for when it is stated, "this is the first and the last," one understands by rule that there must be something remaining in between.

Since that which has nothing before it when something else exists is the "beginning" (ādi), and since that which has nothing after it when something else exists is the "end" (anta), if one were to take [the word] *akāra* and so forth [as the referent], it would follow that the *ikāra*, *ṇakāra*, and others could not possibly be designated as beginning or end.

Here, by the two terms "beginning" and "end," which indicate [something] as a constituent part (*avayava*), the aggregate (*samudāya*) composed of those very parts is implied as the named entity (*saṃjñin*). And because such an aggregate does not occur in usage with respect to a single instance of its application, each individual member is the named entity. However, the final member does not undergo that operation, because it is set aside by the designation *it* and its subsequent elision (*lopa*). This is precisely what is stated in the *Bhāṣya* and in the root text: "and of its own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*).
The interpretation of "svam" as being intended for the purpose of subsequent application (anuvṛtti) is indeed to be rejected; for there would be no purpose in such a subsequent application.
Why [is the word] "iti" used? It is so that a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term) beginning with the letter ṇ—such as "ñamaṅaṇanam"—might not occur.

And because of the inclusion of the word "saha" (together), the designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to the entire collection (*samudāya*); therefore, in cases such as *ikaḥ*, the case-ending arises from the collection itself, not from the initial element alone. Nor is the rule *ādirantyena* (the first [element] together with the last) inconsistent, given that the final element is removed by the designation *it* and its subsequent elision; for even though the *it*-designation occurs within the rules themselves, it does not apply to words like *ig* and so forth. They say that the phrase *antyenā* means "by one similar to the last," which is appropriate precisely under the view of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), and that here the recognition of identity is based solely on similarity.

In the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), although the term *iṇaḥ* alone would have sufficed, the specific mention of *ayvoḥ* indicates that the *iṇ* referred to is only the one following [the letter *ṛ*]; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *laṇ*.

*Halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). Here, there are two distinct words, because if they were compounded, the word *antya* would have been required to stand first according to the rules of compound formation; furthermore, it is established by the style of the Sūtrakāra that words suitable for forming a *karmadhāraya* compound do not enter into such a compound in this instance.

Although every consonant (*hal*) is indeed final with respect to its respective group (*samudāya*), nevertheless, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) between the terms *antya* (final) and *upadeśa* (instruction), what is intended here is that which is final with respect to a group that serves as the object of an enunciation (*uccāraṇa*) intended to make known its own unknown nature.

For this very reason, the letter *u* in *thamuḥ* has fulfilled its purpose as a means of protecting the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the letter *m*. This is because, in all cases, the sages’ intention is directed toward the instruction of the whole (*samudāya-upadeśa*) alone; since the constituent parts (*avayava*) are invariably concomitant [with the whole], they lack the quality of making known their own unknown nature.

"In the *upadeśa*, the final [element]"—this means that which exists there at the end. Consequently, in cases such as *aiuṇ*, the status of *ṇ* and the others as *it* occurs only after the formation of the *hal-pratyāhāra*. However, in other instances, because it is an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation, the *it-saṃjñā* generally applies immediately to what is manifested by pronunciation, without any intervening interval. This is because, as stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *nājjhalau*: "The cognition of the meaning of a word belongs only to that which is divested of its *anubandhas*; the *it-saṃjñā* occurs after the time of the *upadeśa*."

In cases such as *dhut*, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is easily obtained from the form with the *anubandha* (indicatory letter), because that very form—once freed from the *anubandha*—is what presents itself [to the mind] and possesses meaning (*arthavattva*). However, regarding the operation of the technical name *it*, since a name applies only where there is no other meaning, it applies only to that which is presented by the *anubandha*. This is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *titsvaritam*. Furthermore, in the system of grammar, the accent of a *cit* (a term ending in *c*) does not apply here, because although the *c* is similar to the *ic* [of the rule *citaḥ*], it lacks the status of being a *cit*. Moreover, technical names such as "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) apply only to those [suffixes] included within the rules themselves; therefore, rules such as *na vibhaktau* apply only in those specific instances.

For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya—that "in cases such as *idama iś*, the application of the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) which would otherwise result from its being a vowel (*aṇ*), is prohibited by the rule *apratyayaḥ*"—is consistent.

As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *anekāl*—"even in the absence of the mention of *śit* in the case of *iś*, the substitution of the whole [stem] follows simply from the fact that it is marked with *ś*"—the meaning of that is that the status of being a substitute for the whole stem is obtained by taking into account its having been previously (bhūtapūrva) multiliteral due to the presence of the letter *ś* bearing the technical designation *it*; thus, there is no contradiction.

In this regard, some [maintain] that the *anubandhas* are non-exclusive (*anekānta*) and non-limbs (*anavayava*). That which is exclusive (*ekānta*) is never perceived at all; however, this [the *anubandha*] is not like that, because it is never seen when its referent—the element to be enjoined—is present. In the rule *halantyam*, the word *antya* indicates proximity to what follows (*parasamīpa*); in *cuṭū* and similar rules, the word *ādi* indicates proximity to what precedes (*pūrvasamīpa*); and in *anekāl śit* and similar rules, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on the superimposition of being a limb (*avayavatva*) upon proximity, rooted in that very proximity.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *upadeśe'janunāsikaḥ* and from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *maparyantasya*. Consequently, there is no fault regarding [the application of rules] to *ḍā*, *ṇal*, and so forth, as well as to *iś* and so forth. For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *upadeśe* (in the original state of instruction) in the sūtra *upadeśe'c* is purposeful; for that [term] is intended to prevent the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *āditaśca* in cases such as *abhra ām̐ aṭitaḥ*. They say that if [the vowel *a*] were not restricted to its specific context (*anaikāntatva*), then that [prohibition of *iṭ*] would apply.

Others, however, maintain that [the *apṛkta*] is exclusively a single phoneme (*ekānta*), because it is observed as such in the grammatical treatise and is not observed otherwise. For a whole entity such as a crow is perceived in houses, trees, and so forth through its connection with a single class [of objects], but this is not the case here.

Furthermore, if it were a whole entity, then in forms such as *ṇa*, *śa*, and *ka*-suffixes, the substitution of *it* for *ṇ* and the others would not occur, because they would lack the status of being "at the beginning of a suffix" (*pratyayāditva*). Similarly, due to the absence of "being at the end" (*antyatva*), the substitution of *it* for *ś* in forms like *iśādi* would not occur. If one were to resort to figurative interpretation (*lākṣaṇikatva*) for the stated meaning, then the very rule (*lakṣaṇa*) itself would constitute a fault.

Furthermore, because the inclusion of the letter *c* in the rule *daghnaca* would otherwise be rendered purposeless, it is logical that [the *ac*] should indeed be a constituent part [of the suffix]. For this very reason, there is no vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) caused by the *ṇit*-designation of the *ke* suffix prescribed in the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-kaṭhac*. Moreover, since it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* under the rule *tasya lopaḥ* that "being a single unit (*ekāntatva*) is indeed logical," they say that the mention of *upadeśe* (in the original enunciation) in the rule *upadeśe'j-un-as-ud-at-pada-j-anta-kupa-hā-sam-prasāraṇa-an-aṅ-vid-dhātu-vare-ya-lopa-a-vyaya-ghoṣāt-taddhite* is merely for the sake of clarity.

In every case where there is an instruction (*vidhi*) accompanied by a mention of a suffix (*anubandha*), the understanding proceeds in such a manner as: "When [a suffix] having *n* as its technical marker (*itsaṃjñaka*) follows, the letter *s* becomes [the augment *ṣṭun*]," as seen in rules such as *guptijkidbhyaḥ*. In the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), such as in *sanyataḥ*, the understanding proceeds as: "When the word *sa* having *n* as its technical marker follows," and so forth. This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule defining the technical term *niṣṭhā*. For this very reason, the compatibility of rules such as *āṭaśca* is maintained; otherwise, there would be an obvious inconsistency: in the rule for *āṭ*, the condition "when followed by *a*" (*ātparaḥ*) does not exist, yet an increase (*vṛddhi*) is not desired there; whereas in actual usage where an increase is desired, the condition "not followed by *ā*" (*nāṭ*) exists—thus the inconsistency would be evident.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "final" (*antya*)? [It is so that the rule does not apply] to that which is vocalic (*vācāla*). What is the purpose of [specifying] "consonantal" (*hal*)? [It is so that the rule does not apply] to the final [element] of a verbal root (*dhātu*), as in *ciriṇoti* and similar forms. Dr. Rūpāvi: What is the purpose of [specifying] "consonantal"? [It is so that the rule does not apply] to the final [element] of a verbal root in *ciriṇoti* and similar forms.

"Initial utterance" (*ādyocāraṇam*) means the first utterance; this is the sense of the suffix *dhañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). And that [initial utterance] belongs only to the teachers who promulgated the treatise, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Furthermore, "being initial" (*ādyatva*) consists in making known the own-form (*svarūpa*) of something previously unknown. This is because the root *diś-* has the sense of "first," and the act of uttering (*uccāraṇa*) is its action. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated regarding the rule *ekāca upadeśe*: "In the prescription of the technical term *it*, the word 'upadiśati' (he teaches) signifies the act of utterance."

Even in the rule *ādeca* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), it is stated: "The term 'instruction' (*upadeśa*) applies only to those whose form is made known through an utterance not previously heard. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that rule as well, it says: "And for nominal stems (*prātipadika*), there is enumeration (*uddeśa*), not instruction (*upadeśa*). Furthermore, in the commentary on the present rule, it is said: "Instruction is direct verbal communication. As for the argument that [the desired result] is already established by the rule *lājityeva*, that is not correct.

By the rule *ataddhite*, it is understood that the letter *l* (the marker for *taddhita* suffixes) does not possess the quality of being an *it*. It should also be noted that if *astāti* and *as* were treated as having the quality of an *it*, then in the case of *athastāt*, there would be the undesirable application of *jaśtva* by the rule *siti ca*, and in the case of *avastāt*, there would be the undesirable application of *lopaś śākalyasya*. The question "Why [is the word] *hal*? is asked because [the desired result] could be established through the previously mentioned *yogavibhāga* and other means used to avoid mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). The answer is given with the intention that such a method would be overly cumbersome (*gurubhūta*): "It moves from *ciriṇ*" (*ciriṇa etīti*). The implication is that if that were the case, the augment *num* would occur.

It should not be argued that, because the term *jhal* is extracted from the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* and interpreted as "the augment *num* applies to a verbal root ending in *jhal*," the designation *it* does not apply to the vowel *i* (as in *na cet*) since this is the result of its being non-initial (*nāditva*); for it must be stated that the extraction of *jhal* is necessary in the rule *ugidacām*, otherwise *num* would fail to apply in cases such as *dhinoti*.

"Direct statement" (*pratyakṣākhyāna*) refers to that which has the scripture alone as its object and consists in being conducive to a cognition whose qualificandum-ness is delimited by words uttered by the three sages. This "delimitation" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) occurs through two relations: (1) being the property of the verbal cognition produced by itself, and (2) being delimited by a property that serves as the delimitor of the object-ness of the mental presentation produced by itself. As for the view that the essence [of a direct statement] is the state of being an operation qualified by a property, through the dual relation of (1) being conducive to a verbal cognition whose qualificandum-ness is delimited by itself, and (2) being conducive to a perception whose qualifier is itself—[that is not correct].

That is not so, because [the technical name *upadeśa*] does not exist when the augment *ṅmuṭ* is uttered. Rejecting the view of the ancients—that the word *upadeśa* ends in the abstract suffix *ghañ* and that it is connected with what follows—he establishes that it ends in the instrumental suffix *ghañ* and is not connected with what follows, by means of the words "But others... and so on. The question "What is meant by *upadeśa*? is a question concerning the scope of the present subject matter. [The example is: *abhra ām̐ apa*.

Although one might easily argue that this is so because there is no result [of the rule] in that case, nevertheless, since the result is easily stated in the case of *abhra āṭitaḥ*—where [the application of the rule] would otherwise be non-conclusive—it should be understood that this [example] is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). As for the phrase "after *lūṭ* as well": one should not say that the insertion of *it* is easily obtained because the two suffixes are indeed mentioned in the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*.

By stating that the offspring related to the meaning of another word has an unexpressed nature as a remainder (*śeṣa*), it is accepted that even in the present case, these two—*śatṛ* and *śānac*—which are distinct from those [suffixes] connected with being substitutes for *laṭ* and so forth, are presented by the term *sat*. Consequently, there is no lack of direct manifestation (*pratyakṣākhyāna*) regarding them.

Nor should it be argued that since the rule is already established by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, the explicit mention of those two again serves merely to refer back to those two as they appeared previously—characterized by the letter *ś* and so forth, which bear the technical name *it*—and thus, by prescribing them with the word *sat* (present participle), there is no necessity for their re-application in this subsequent context. For if that were the case, since those two suffixes would still possess their connection to being substitutes for *laṭ* and so forth in the previous instance, one would have to refer back to them precisely as qualified by those properties; this would lead to many complications, whereas what must be referred back is their form alone.

This has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The mention of *tau* is for the purpose of [excluding] non-connection. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states that only the forms of *śatṛ* and *śānac* are referred to. And thus, it should be understood that once a rule has prescribed [an element], the designation *it* must necessarily follow. [The word] *niṣṭhā* means...

Nor should it be argued that, because the *sūtra* and *bhāṣya* on "niṣṭhā" provide the designation *niṣṭhā* for the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* as characterized by the letter *k* (which serves as an indicator), and since these two alone are prescribed by the term *niṣṭhā*, there is no need for the application of the present rule here; for the prescription of those two occurs within the context of the *niṣṭhā* designation, and [the rule] applies to those two once they have been so prescribed.

Regarding the term *niṣṭhā-saṃjñā*, in order to avoid mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—according to the maxim of the "cloth and the weaving" (*sūtra-śāṭaka-nyāya*)—it is necessary that those two [suffixes] exist for which the designation *niṣṭhā* is prescribed. Since there is no status as an original enunciation (*upadeśatva*) for those now designated as *niṣṭhā*, and since the designation *itsaṃjñā* (the *it*-designation) cannot be applied to what is qualified by the letter *k* and so on in the absence of *ittva* (the *it*-quality), it is necessary that the application of *ittva* occurs for those [suffixes] that have been prescribed.

Furthermore, this cannot be a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) in the sense that "the suffixes *-tṛ* and *-tavat* do not apply where a *niṣṭhā* suffix applies," because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the *it*-designation (the marker *i*) would not apply to the constituent parts of the suffixes *śatṛ*, *śānac*, and *taktavat* when they are prescribed [by rules such as P. 3.2.124]. Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the *it*-designation would not apply to the initial consonants of suffixes like *kyap*, which are inferred from nipātanas (irregular formations) such as "rājasūya-sūrya" and "cityāgni-citye. However, the form of the root *vad* mentioned in the rule "badhaḥ supi" (P. 3.2.61) does not belong to this [category of *niṣṭhā*].

For this very reason, in the *Nyāsa* commentary on the rule "tasyāpatyam ata iñ," it is stated in the authoritative source (*ākara*) that the meaning of "offspring" connected with the word "anya" (in the compound *anyāpatyam*) possesses the status of being a remainder (*śeṣa*) whose form has not been explicitly stated. Therefore, in this sūtra, it must be stated that by the term *upadeśa*, *uddeśa* (the enunciation) is also included. [Objection: If so, then [the suffix] would also apply in cases such as *abhraām̐ apaḥ*; thus, their inclusion [in the scope of the rule] and the exclusion [of others] from it [must be specified]. What is that specific condition (*viśeṣa*) by which [this distinction] occurs? This is the question.

For the sake of subsuming those two [the *saṃjñā* and *paribhāṣā*] under a single category, their commingling is accepted even through worldly convention; furthermore, the status of being an "instruction" (*upadeśatva*) is admitted for both, just as it is for recurrent rules (*anuvṛtti*), provided that the term *it* is easily available. If this were the case, however, all *saṃjñā*-rules would—by an identical logic—result in being *paribhāṣā*s, which would lead to the collapse of the very category of *saṃjñā*-rules. Consequently, the word *niṣṭhā* would fail to function as the determinant of the objective domain (*viṣayatā*) of cognition in its respective instances.

Furthermore, because nowhere is there seen any gender (liṅga) consisting of words forming part of a sūtra that serves merely to bring about the application of a technical definition (paribhāṣā) without being a motivator for the production of a grammatical form; and because it would result in the redundancy of specifying different case-endings after the word *niṣṭhā* in various instances; and because of the difficulty involved in assuming that the case-ending attached to the indicator (upasthāpaka) must be construed with the indicated object (upasthāpya) based on contextual implication (sāmarthya); and because it would entail the violation of the rule that suffixes must invariably connect with the meaning of their own base (prakṛti). [Otherwise], the shortening of the vowel in the root *pā-* would not occur.

The sense is that there is complexity (*gaurava*) in the inference [of the rule] due to the technical designation *itsaṃjñā*. As for the objection that there would be the fault of the non-occurrence of the *it* designation for the elements contained within the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) suffixes in the examples "kālebhyo bhavavat" and "caraṇebhyo dharmavat," that is not correct. Since it can be stated that the extension applies only to those very elements characterized by their respective *it* designations when prescribed in the sense of "originating from" (*bhava*) and so forth, the re-application of the *it* designation is not necessary here. Furthermore, in that context, the extension must necessarily apply only to those elements connected with the base (*prakṛti*) and so on; such is the direction of the argument.

Regarding the term *ākara*: in the rule *tasyāpatyam ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), since the offspring related to the meaning of the word ending in *a* is already expressed by that [suffix], the offspring related to the meaning of the word *bhānu* remains unexpressed. Consequently, as that [offspring] is the "remainder," the suffix *cha* applies according to the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114). Thus, the suffix *cha* follows from the word *bhānu*. It is stated therein that this is for the purpose of a formal separation (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule. Regarding the phrase "by worldly usage" (*lokavyavahāreṇa*): it means by such usages as "the lesson (*anuvāka*) has been assigned to me" or "the path has been taught to me."

[Objection: But surely, since the vowel *ā* is also an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the pronunciation of *ā*, there would be a fault even when [the suffix] *ghañ* is added to an instrument; therefore, he says: "They are instruments for the instruction of what is being employed. This means they are the instruments for the instruction regarding the correctness (*sādhutva*) of that which is being employed as a finished form. [The phrase] "composed by the Blessed One" implies that it is improper to conceive of a construction that contradicts the Bhāṣya. Having thus generally refuted the view that [the suffix] *ghañ* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*), he says, starting with "Furthermore," with the intention that such a [view] would be all the more faulty if it were carried over into the subsequent rule.

In order to prevent the substitution of *it* (short *i*) for the final vowel of each individual member of such a collection, it is necessary to define the term as "the final member of a collection that is the locus of the complete fulfillment of the intentionality (*tātparya*) directed toward the utterance of a signifier whose own form was previously unknown. Since, in cases involving a dual compound (*dvandva*), it is necessary to assume an intentionality directed toward the utterance of the entire collection—following the maxim of the movement of a tree (where the whole moves)—the utterance of the individual members is merely incidental; therefore, there is no necessity for an intentionality directed toward those individual parts.

The meaning is this: since the state of being the locus where such an intentionality is fully instantiated (paryāptyadhikaraṇatā) exists only in the entire aggregate, the property of being the final member of such an aggregate does not exist in the letter *ka* and so on; therefore, the designation *it* (the short vowel *i*) would not apply. This is what he indicates by the words "of the other" (*parasya*), etc. By this, it is shown that being the final member of the aggregate being taught consists in being a constituent of that aggregate while not occurring at the moment preceding the constituent letters of that aggregate.

Having postulated the intention of the root text—that while there is existence of the qualifier by taking the suffix *ṭhak*, there is an absence of the qualified object by taking the suffix *cha*—if one were to argue that, on account of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one must postulate an intention for each individual utterance in a place where a *dvandva* compound is used, in order to secure the status of being a predicate for each member individually, that is not correct.

Although it is necessary for each individual intention (*tātparya*)—namely, "let the word *ṭhak* be the indicator of the suffix *ṭhak*" and "let the word *chas* be the indicator of the suffix *chas*"—to secure the status of being the object of prescription (*vidheyatā*), nevertheless, in the case of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), there is also the necessity of an intention such as "let the word *ṭhakchasa* be the indicator of both *ṭhak* and *chas* as delimited by their conjunction," or "let the collection of *ṭhak* and *chas* residing in the compound be the indicator. It is accepted that precisely such an intention is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the utterance of the aforementioned collection, because it underlies all those respective utterances.

The individual intentions [of the speakers] are not the motivators for that [utterance], because when the utterance is possible by virtue of an intention directed toward the collective whole, one does not accept the individual, non-uniform intentions as motivators due to their complexity (*gaurava*). Nor should it be argued that even the utterance of each individual [word] is prompted by the intention toward the whole, and thus the property of being a "whole" (which is the object of such an intention) exists in each individual [word].

This is because we intend to define [the locus] as the substratum where the complete distribution (*paryāpti*) of such an intentionality resides; since that [intentionality] does not exist in each individual [element], a flaw is inevitable. Furthermore, in order to prevent the shortening of the vowel *i* (*ittva*) from applying to the final element of each respective collection, it is necessary to include the concept of "complete distribution" (*paryāpta*). For this very reason, in cases involving the intentionality of a sentence (*vākya*), the individual [word-level] objectivities of cognition are untenable. This is the general direction of the argument.

He states that such a means—which would render the continuation of the word *upadeśapada* (the term "instruction") from the previously mentioned [sūtra] useless as a way of avoiding the aforementioned defects—is not to be resorted to because it serves merely as a means for establishing the state of being a "bhāva" (an action/state). He does so with the words beginning with *yadi tu*. The phrase *ata eva* means "precisely because there is no result in the final analysis. Anticipating the objection that the continuation of the word *upadeśapada* ending in the instrumental case (*karaṇaghañanta*) contradicts the Vārttika, he refutes it with the words beginning with *na ca*. This [refutation] extends up to the portion of the text beginning with *yattu kiṃcit*.

And this was rejected by the author of the Bhāṣya on the grounds of the inclusion of the term "final" (antyagrahaṇa). In that regard, the description—found in the subsequent sūtra—that the word *upadeśa* does not carry over because roots and so forth are qualified by their *anubandhas*, must be disregarded as it contradicts the context of this very work. [The phrase] "it simply does not arise" [is the conclusion].

If it were stated that "the final [letter] is [the substitute] in the case of instruction (*upadeśane*)," then by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the meaning "that which is final to it" would be obtained, and thus the Vārttika would not arise. For me, however, since the first utterance cannot have a final [element], it is impossible to rely on proximity; therefore, the Vārttika arises because the meaning "of whichever [element] is final to the aggregate" is necessitated. Even if proximity could somehow be established, the status of being an aggregate subject to the first utterance exists for each individual member as well; this is the reason for its arising. [The phrase] "by way of the aggregate" means: [The meaning is: By way of the aggregate, that which is the final element of the aggregate is the substitute for the first utterance. If one were to say "in the case of instruction," then by proximity, the meaning "final to that" would be understood, and the Vārttika would be unnecessary. But for me, since the first utterance cannot have a final [element], proximity cannot be resorted to; thus, the Vārttika arises through the implication that it refers to whatever is the final element of the aggregate. Even if some sort of proximity were possible, the property of being an aggregate subject to the first utterance exists in each individual part as well, and that is why the Vārttika arises. [The expression] "by way of the aggregate" [is used].

The *Vārttika* was composed by establishing that even the constituent parts (*avayava*) possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) through a traditional succession; otherwise, there would be a mutual contradiction between the two *Vārttikas*. The intention of the *Vārttika* is that the enumeration [of specific sounds] is solely for the purpose of excluding those not relevant to the context. Regarding the phrase "by the force of the mention of the final [sound]," some hold that it does not serve to exclude the initial [sound], because such exclusion is already possible through the restrictive rule itself, namely *cuṭū* (Pāṇini 1.3.7).

In reality, since the word "all" (*sarva*) is employed in the Bhāṣya in the statement "every consonant is the final element with respect to its respective group," it is appropriate to explain the intention as follows: even an initial [consonant] possesses the status of being "final" by virtue of the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (designation as if it were the principal); therefore, there is no exclusion of such initials by the term "final" (*antya*). Furthermore, in this way, it appears that even the burden of complexity resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) does not exist.

One might object: "Since the *bhāṣya* on the rule *na dhātulopaḥ* establishes that only a verbal root (*dhātu*) stripped of its *anubandhas* can possess the status of a *dhātu*, it follows that a *dhātu* cannot be the cause for the designation *it*. Therefore, this enumeration [of causes] is entirely irrelevant. To this, he replies with the words beginning "In that case" (*tatra*). The point is that here, the status of being a *dhātu* and so forth is of a different nature altogether. Furthermore, it is appropriate to say that in the sentence of the enumeration, the word "root" (*dhātu*) and others refer to that which makes known the roots and so forth.

For this very reason, since the rule *lopaśca* indicates a substitute (*ādeśa*) by virtue of its incorporated *ś*, and since in the alternative view that *ṅamo hrasvāt* consists of two words—*um* and *uḍ*—it indicates an augment (*āgama*), it follows that there is no lack of established status (*asiddhi*) for the *ś* and *ṭ* sounds, as in the case of [the rule regarding] *śakāra* and *ṭakāra*. This is not so; however, it should be understood that [the term *avyaya*] is not composed of elements suitable for being verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth. Because particles (*nipāta*) are indicative (*dyotaka*), they are treated separately according to the *brāhmaṇavasiṣṭha-nyāya*. And Kaiyaṭa says that "determination" (*vyavasitatva*) consists in being delimited by the status of being a verbal root and so forth. And thus, [the final letter of] nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as *udaśvit*...

If this were the case, the phrase "of those not ending in *kṛt* or *taddhita*" in the Vārttika—"there is a prohibition of nominal stems [from taking the feminine suffix] if they do not end in *kṛt* or *taddhita*"—would be redundant. Furthermore, to assign a different meaning to such a Vārttika would violate the natural sense of the words. Moreover, since terms like *kṛt* indicate the suffixes beginning with them, the letter *t* would incur the status of being an *it* (indicatory), resulting in the accentuation of the *ti*-accent for all *ku*-suffixes, because the *it*-status residing in the indicator (*bodhaka*) is superimposed upon that which is indicated (*bodhya*). Nor should it be argued that the *rit*-status of suffixes like *anīyar* would be useless.

In this regard, it could also be argued that there is an annulment (*bādha*) by the specific rule regarding the suffix *rittva*. Furthermore, since the meaningfulness of the *cakāra* in *tṛcaḥ* is possible through such a method, the Bhāṣyakāra’s demonstration of the uselessness (*vaiyarthya*) of the *cakāra* in *caḥ* would be entirely irrelevant. Nor should it be said that the *takāra* in *tavyat* is useless; for its presence serves a purpose, namely to prevent the application of the prohibition in the rule *pūraṇaguṇa-*. This is because the *takāra* would otherwise serve as a qualifier in forms such as *idyati*.

Furthermore, since *tiṅ* suffixes function as indicators (*bodhaka*) of a grammatical operation, if the rule *usyapadāntāt* were to apply, there would be no occurrence of *guṇa* in forms such as *bhaviṣīṣṭa*; the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* would instead apply for the sake of forms like *śyan*. If one were to prevent this through an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) or similar means, it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Moreover, regarding the phrase *lopaśca*, the *śas* therein indicates that the entire [stem] is to be replaced (*sarvādeśatā*), rather than indicating a specific substitute (*ādeśa*); thus, its status as a substitute (*tatrasthatva*) is difficult to establish. Similarly, even under the interpretation that *muṭ* consists of two distinct words, it does not possess the character of an augment (*āgama-bodhakatva*).

However, let the detailed discussion rest here: that which is uttered in connection with *vas* (the suffix of the present participle) conveys the status of being the first member [of a compound]. Now, an objection is raised: since it is desired that even meaningless particles (*nipāta*) receive the designation of *prātipadika*, their status as *prātipadika*s would already be established by that very definition; therefore, the separate mention of particles is redundant. To this, he says: "by the maxim of the Brāhmaṇa and Vasiṣṭha. This means: because they are delimited by their status as verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth; that is to say, because they are taught by the author of the treatise (*śāstrakṛt*) as such.

It should be understood that the indicator (*gamaka*) of the author’s intention (*tātparya*) to convey the specific [meaning] as the actual reality (*tattva*) is precisely the letter *th* in *thamu*. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is bound by the nature of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and so forth, because it is composed of those [elements]. Thus, having resolved the contradiction with the Vārttika that arose in his own system, he demonstrates the contradiction with the Vārttika regarding the subsequent recurrence of the term *upadeśa* ending in the suffix *bhāva-ghañ*, starting with the words "And thus... (*evañca*).

Since it was previously established that the subsequent passage beginning with "na ca" (nor [is there]) cannot arise if the preceding text intends to demonstrate a lack of recurrence, such an introduction would be incoherent; furthermore, it does not conform to the literal meaning of the words "evañca" (and thus). Regarding the phrase "of the nominal stems" (*prātipadikānām*): one should not argue that this [rule] would result in the prohibition of *citra* and so forth, for this would only be logical here if the designation *it* were not applied due to the absence of the effect of *it*.

The teachers maintain that when a specific meaning [of a suffix] occurs, it receives that designation; for example, in the case of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, they become *agasti* and *kuṇḍina*. This is because, at the commencement of the *vārttika* by means of the subsequent commentary (*taduttarabhāṣya*)—which aims to show that the letter *c* in *kuṇḍina* would not receive the designation *it*—this very fault has already been addressed. Śrīdhara, however, offers a solution by relying on a *madhyamapadalopa* compound (meaning "those whose *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes are not heard" refers to those ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes that are not heard), thus asserting that the prohibition applies only to those ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes that are not actually heard.

As for the refutation of Śrīdhara’s statement that [the rule] contradicts Kaiyaṭa because Kaiyaṭa has stated that *udaśvit* and other such forms are *avyutpanna* (non-etymologically derived), that is not correct. For the contradiction with Kaiyaṭa does not undermine the authority [of the rule], and it is also possible to maintain that the said Vārttika was formulated with the intention of [excluding only those items] that possess etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, as for the phrase "those which possess the denotative capacity qualified by being understood through the function of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-vṛtti*)," the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is established by both relations: being delimited by the form that delimits itself (*svāvacchedaka-rūpa*), and being related to itself (*svanirūpitatva*).

Therefore, there is no room for the previously mentioned objection. Alternatively, the meaning is: "of those [words] which are the causes of the objective condition (*viṣayatā*) delimited by the sequence [found] in their own occurrence as nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Or again, the meaning is: "of those [words] qualified as nominal stems by two relations: being the cause of a cognition having itself as its object, and not being composed of that which is not a constituent part of itself. The expression "not a kṛt suffix," etc., serves merely to capture the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Nor is there any fault even in these three interpretations regarding such rules as *udaśvito 'nyatarasyām*.

It should not be argued that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) because the status of being expressive (*bodhakatva*) residing in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which depends on the absence of the designation *it* (*itsaṃjñā*) and elision (*lopa*), requires the absence of those two (*itsaṃjñā* and *lopa*), which in turn is required by the prohibition [of the designation *it*] triggered by that very status. Rather, what is meant is that the possibility of the status of being expressive—qualified by expressiveness residing in the nominal stem—is triggered by the possibility of the absence of the designation *it* and elision. It is this [possibility] that...

The author of the *Vārttika* stated: "Of those ending in *dvitā*. [He argued that] in examples such as *kumbhakāraḥ*, since the general rule (*utsarga*) applies only after setting aside the scope of the exception (*apavāda*), the suffix *ṇa* and others would not be elided if the word were a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) prior [to the addition of the suffix]. To this, he said "not when followed by a *kṛt* suffix," and so forth. However, that [objection] was rejected in the *Bhāṣya* on the grounds that there is no practical result, stating "it is not necessary," etc., because there is no fault since the form *payāṇām* is intended [by the author].

They say that because we observe the usage of forms such as *udaśvit-katipaya* (where *udaśvit* occurs with the suffix *ka*) and the non-usage of forms such as *citraka* (where *citra* occurs with the suffix *ka*), both the possibility and impossibility [of such formations] are conceivable. However, even that is not correct; for it is inappropriate to assume that [the word] *akṛt* and so forth functions merely as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). In this view, there would be an inconsistency with the subsequent Bhāṣya, which takes the faultiness of the form *kuṇḍinac* as its intended meaning.

Furthermore, since it could be argued that in constructions such as *rāja-śvaśura-* and *āditya-*, the base ending in *-an* (as in *rājā*) is also obtained [by the rule], the substitution of *it* for the *n* in the word *rājan* would be unavoidable. To justify this through an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) or similar means would be burdened by excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, it appears that the solution stated by the Teacher alone is the correct one.

Now, since in your view the presentation of a word-meaning as being free from its suffixal appendages (*anubandha*) is accepted, one might argue that in cases such as *kumbhakāra*, at the time the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is applied, the suffixes like *ṇa* are not yet present; therefore, [rules concerning] *akaḍ* and so forth would be redundant. To this, he replies with the words "In *kumbhakāra* etc. Here, by the word "etc.," it should be understood that the forms *āśabda* (derived from the root *aś* with the suffix *vic*) and *īśabda* (derived from the form *āśabda* with the suffix *in*) are included. [The phrase] "by avoiding the domain of exceptions" means...

The statement "the presentation of a word-meaning free from its suffixes" (*anubandhavinirmuktapadārthopasthiti*) is not an independent injunction; rather, it is obtained through the initial application of the technical names (*saṃjñā*) such as *antaraṅga* and the elision (*lopa*). And so, in the present case, by the principle of what is about to be applied (*upasañjaniṣyamāṇanyāya*), since the technical name *it* and the elision have not yet occurred previously, the rule applies to that very form qualified by them in the actual linguistic object (*lakṣya*). Thus, the sense is that the phrase "not in a *kṛt* [suffix]" (*akṛt*) and so forth is intended to set aside the prohibition that would otherwise apply there.

In this context, restriction (*saṅkoca*) should be understood as [applying] to the meaning of the term *upadeśa* by excluding what is other than a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), or to the meaning of the term *hal* by excluding a *hal* that is not the final one of a nominal stem. By this, the statement of the Teacher (Patañjali) that "the presentation of the word-meaning devoid of its markers (*anubandha*) is improper because it would contradict this [rule]" is refuted, on the grounds that there is no [undesired] consequence (*phala*).

Because of the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) here, one must carry forward the word *pratyayāt* from the rule *bhīhībhṛhadajyarti...* [P. 6.1.193] and transform it into its locative case (*pratyaye*) to qualify *nit-* in the rule *litī* [P. 6.1.193], just as in that previous instance; thus, the absence of any result [from this specific application] should be understood from other sources. Now, an objection might be raised: based on the Bhāṣya in the *Paspaśāhnika*, where the word *upadeśa*—meaning "enunciation for the purpose of non-sublation"—is carried forward [from P. 1.3.2], this Vārttika would not even arise, since it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *ādeca upadeśe* [P. 6.1.45]: "There is enunciation (*uddeśa*) of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), but no enunciation (*upadeśa*)."

In accordance with the syntactic unity of this statement with the *Bhāṣya* located at the end of the *Paspaśāhnika*, which says, "The teaching (*upadeśa*) of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that are not [already] grasped must be performed, lest there be forms such as *mañcaka* and *mañjaka*," it should be understood that the word *upadeśa* in the *Bhāṣya* means "the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*) must be performed. Furthermore, it should be noted that this [act of grasping] is merely in the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*), serving to remove doubt.

But if this were so, then according to the view that the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe* (P. 1.1.66) serves to determine the application of the genitive case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the genitive being applied even in cases such as *guptijkidbhyaḥ* (P. 3.1.5). Nor can it be argued that there is no such obstacle because the suffix *san* itself will be the substitute for *san*, since it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "When 'in the original instruction' (*upadeśe*) is mentioned, the designation *it* is determined"; thus, one might claim that the word *upadeśa* does not recur here. This is not correct, because that statement is merely the opinion of a partial authority (*ekadeśin*) and therefore lacks proving power.

Since even the name [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*] is obtained as an "instruction" (*upadeśa*), there is no reason for the *Vārttika* not to arise; therefore, he says: "And the enunciation," and so forth. Now, one might ask: what is the status of the *Bhāṣya* located in the *Paspaśā*? To this, he connects that *Bhāṣya* with the words beginning "This *Bhāṣya*," and so on. Regarding the phrase "the word 'instruction'": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that sentence in which the word 'instruction' occurs. The sense is that the word "instruction" [is used in the sense] "the instruction is to be performed"; thus, there is no fault of syntactic inconsistency with the phrase "it is not to be performed."

[Objection: But even so, does it not still result in being an *upadeśa* (instruction)? To this he says: "And that is a restatement (*anuvāda*). The sense is that because it lacks the quality of making known its own nature as something previously unknown, it cannot be an *upadeśa*. Having raised the objection regarding a contradiction with the Bhāṣya—both in the case where the word *upadeśa* is understood in the instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*) and in the case where it is not understood at all—he resolves it with the words beginning "But if this were so... [and so forth]. Regarding the phrase "san becomes san": the sense is that since the *san* inferred from the restatement of *san* is the closest [by the principle of *antaratama*], the substitute will indeed be *san*. This is said while the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is being employed.

The meaning is that [the word] "upadeśa" (in the original rule) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over), and thus it refers to what is being prescribed [at that time]. [The phrase] "it should not be assumed" [refers to] that which is obtained through the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning the closest substitute).

For instance, in the *Tantra* [the *Mahābhāṣya*], regarding rules such as "ṅamo hrasvād aci," where both the seventh and fifth case endings are specified, a doubt arises as to whether the operation applies to the preceding element or the following one. In response, the Siddhāntin states that between these two, the specification by the fifth case is stronger due to its being subsequent (*paratva*) and lacking an opportunity for application (*anavakāśatva*). Thereupon, the Ekadeśin offers another solution, stating that "or rather, a genitive specification should be made according to the actual sense. The meaning of this is that, in accordance with the specific context among the aforementioned cases, the operands (*kāryin*) should be indicated by the sixth case ending.

Since the mention of the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśa*) is required in some instances before [the rule] and in others after it, this statement of a partial proponent (*ekadeśy-ukti*)—which avoids the burden of mentioning both—is made. Subsequently, another partial proponent rejects that statement by asserting that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) itself is determined by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī-pada*) from the preceding rule, and thus relying on the principle that "the genitive is used according to the sense" (*yathārthā vā ṣaṣṭhī*), he maintains that the rule beginning with *tasmin* alone is what establishes the genitive.

Since there is a risk of complexity (*gaurava*) due to the recurrence of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and in order to prevent both [the preceding and following elements] from being simultaneously designated as the *prakalpaka*, one must accept that either priority (*paratva*) or lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*) applies. Furthermore, because the mention of "both the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) in the rule *pūrvaparayoḥ* serves as a necessary indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of simultaneous designation, this too is free from doubt. Nor should it be argued that there is no room for doubt regarding the meaning "of the vowel following the word *man* and of the neutral (*udāsīna*) vowel preceding it," and thus the statement "due to priority" (*paratvāt*) is untenable; for there is no contradiction [in such an interpretation].

Regarding the rule *ṅama uttarasyāco 'ci parataḥ*, there is doubt because of the authority of the *Bhāṣya*, which states that "the term *ṅam* [indicates] doubt. This is because, by assuming an absence of intent (*tātparya*) toward neutral cases, both doubt and contradiction exist; furthermore, in examples such as *idāsaḥ*—which are included under the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—doubt and contradiction necessarily exist. For instance, in that context, the term *aṅgasya* (of the base) is understood to carry over, and by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it must be taken as referring specifically to that which is caused by the augment *āṭ*.

Thus, since there is no possibility of anything being replaced by *īda* between these two constituent parts (*aṅga*), there exists a doubt or conflict as to whether it is the preceding or the following element that is eliminated. As for that which [is applied] to the portions presented by this *paribhāṣā*:

They have resolved [the issue] as follows: where both [elements] are not mentioned—such as in the case of *siddha*, *niṣphala*, or *bādhita*—there is no presentation of those parts; whereas in a place where both are indicated by the genitive case (e.g., *ṣaṣṭhyaṃśa*), since there is no fruit [of distinction], and because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) for why the presentation should be by one rather than the other, they justify the occurrence of both. However, that [explanation] is to be disregarded because it does not conform to the words of the Bhāṣya, which state: "There is doubt whether [the rule applies to] the vowel following *ṅam*, or to the vowel preceding *aci*. Regarding the phrase "in some cases, *pūrva-tra*": this refers to rules such as *ānemuṭ* and *turiṣṭhemeyasu*.

The phrase "somewhere later on" refers to instances such as *trestrayaḥ* and *maya ujaḥ*. This mention of both [the base and the suffix] is a statement made by a partisan (ekadeśin) in the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara* accompanied by the grace of the Guru (*Guruprasāda*). Following that, a fault was raised against that position by another partisan who adheres to the preceding view, regarding forms such as *guptijityādi*. Then, the partisan who maintains the application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīpraklaptivādin*) stated: "This fault would indeed arise if the designation *it* were to wait for the substitute; however, once the designation *it* has been applied and the elision (*lopa*) performed, the substitute will occur. For the designation *it* is said to apply to what is taught (*upadeśa*). Thus, the intention is that your statement is refuted.

With the intention that this does not follow the instructions of the *Upadeśapada*, [the author] provides another resolution: "Alternatively, as long as the suffix *san* has not arisen, there cannot be an application (*praklapti*) [of the rule]; and when *san* has arisen, since the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) has already been accounted for, there will be no such application."

Thus [ends the quote]. The sense is "according to what is appropriate. Having thus restated that Bhāṣya—which intends to show that the recurrence of the word *upadeśapada* ending in the suffix *bhāva*-lyuṭ is merely the statement of a partial view (*ekadeśin*)—he restates the subsequent Bhāṣya, beginning with "syādeṣa doṣaḥ" (this fault might arise), while suggesting that, on the contrary, the recurrence of the word *upadeśapada* ending in the suffix *karaṇa*-lyuṭ is also established by this very Bhāṣya. This is the intention of the Bhāṣya here:

If the word *upadeśa* were understood as "that which teaches the existence [of an element]" (*bhāvasādhana*), then since the *san* inferred by the rule of repetition (*anuvāda*) would lack the status of being an *upadeśa*, the substitution of *s* for *san* would not occur; consequently, because the quality of *it*-ness (*ittva*) would be required for that substitute, the fault you pointed out would arise. However, if the word *upadeśa* is understood as "the instrument of teaching" (*karaṇasādhana*), then even the *san* inferred by the rule of repetition is a suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, since its *it*-designation and elision (*lopa*) are applied first due to its internal nature (*antaraṅga*), it will be replaced by itself based on phonetic similarity (*āntaratamya*); thus, the quality of *t*-ness (*tattva*) is not required. This interpretation of the intent of the Bhāṣya is indeed correct.

Otherwise, there would arise the inconsistency of writing [the word *upadeśa*] again as a means to avoid that fault, since the sentence "this is called *itihā*" would then be intended merely to demonstrate the reason for the absence of other [causes] for what was previously stated. For me, however, there is no inconsistency, because in the preceding sentence the word *upadeśa* is used in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*), whereas in the subsequent one it is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*).
