One might raise the following objection: "Since the fault has already been avoided in the view that the *bhāṣya* statement 'nanu syādeṣa' intends the suffix as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), the pursuit of the alternative view beginning with 'athavā' is redundant. Therefore, the alternative view introduced by 'athavā' must be understood as referring to the view that the suffix is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Keeping this doubt in mind, [the author] quotes the subsequent *bhāṣya* starting with 'athavā', with the underlying intention that, in reality, the non-continuation of the word 'upadeśa' is ultimately obtained from this very *bhāṣya*."

By this, since the status of being a statement by a partial exponent (*ekadeśin*) is already established by what was previously stated, the passage beginning with *syādeṣa* and ending with *kaiyaṭa āha* serves as an exposition of the present subject. In that context, Kaiyaṭa says that because the ablative case is exhausted in the production of the suffix *san* as qualified by "priority" (*paratva*), and because there is no other application [of the rule], that [ablative] does not possess the capacity to provide a basis for the operation (*prakalpakatva*). This is its meaning.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assume that the *Bhāṣya-vārttika*—which is situated within the present *sūtra* and composed with the desire to explain the meaning of that *sūtra*—is a mere *prauḍhivāda* (an assertion made for the sake of argument) on the strength of that particular portion of the *Bhāṣya*. This is because the linguistic forms (*lakṣya*) would otherwise remain unestablished. For instance, [the items] such as *aiuṇ* possess meaningfulness by virtue of indicating a sequence, and thus they possess the status of *prātipadika* (nominal stems). Likewise, [the elements] such as *citraṅ* and *cuḥ kuḥ* also possess the status of *prātipadika*. Even in the case of the rule *lopaśca*, the *śakāra* possesses meaningfulness in its own form, and therefore it possesses the status of *prātipadika*.

If the substitutes (*anubandhas*) were exclusively single-consonant (*ekānta*), then, while the mention of *lopa* from the rule "lopo yi" continues to apply, the explicit mention of *lup* again indicates that it is a total substitute (*sarvādeśa*). Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule "ekāca upadeśe" is indeed questionable, as is any other similar view. [The rule] "ekāca upadeśe..."

The doubt that [the argument] is useless has been dispelled. "And thus" (*evam ca*) means: once it is established that the position of the partial proponent—which maintains that [the word] is a *bhāva-sādhana* (denoting an action)—is merely a statement of a partisan, and that in reality such a status does not apply. "In the present context" (*prakṛta*) means: because the primary subject matter (*prakaraṇa*) carries greater weight. "Regarding the meaning of the Sūtra" (*sūtrārtha*) means: it is proper to determine the meaning by means of that which is intent upon explaining the meaning itself, and not by means of a mere refutation of another's view within a different incidental context.

It should be understood that although the intent of refuting the *parokti* (the opponent's statement) is equal in both cases, here [in our view], the intent is to establish the meaning relevant to the context (*prākaraṇika*), which serves as the means for ensuring the validity of the rule. Regarding the phrase "and because the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) would not be established": the meaning is that if the *it*-designation were not applied to those forms prescribed by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* (P. 3.2.124), then the illustrative examples such as *vakṣyamāṇā* and others would fail to be established. Now, one might object: "In your system as well, since forms such as *aiuṇ* are not included among those specifically enumerated, the failure to establish the illustrative examples is common to both parties. To this, he says: "And [the rule] *lopaśca*... [is the solution].

But surely, since the suffix *nan* is an integral part of the indicator (*bodhaka*), it cannot possess the capacity to indicate its own form, just as the letter *r* does not indicate itself in words such as *rāma*. Thus, one might raise the objection: "In that case, how can it have the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? Anticipating this, he states that in this view, [the application of the rule] is simply not required: "Of the indicatory letters" (*anubandhānām*), etc. Now, one might object that the rule *ekāca upadeśe* ("a monosyllabic root in its original enunciation") is supported by Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the Sūtra and implies a verbal derivation (bhāva-janta). To this he replies: "ekāca," etc. The reading is *upadeśe'vata* and so forth. [The rule] *ādeca*... [is cited].

In the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara* accompanied by the *Guruprasāda*, however, the wise have explained that in rules such as "ādeca upadeśe," the term [ādi] is used exclusively in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*). Thus they say.
The reading "tvap" is a corruption, because it functions as the object of the action. Thus they say.

As for the objection that others [raise] regarding the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*, since the word *tau* refers to those two [suffixes] specifically characterized by the letter *ś* which bears the technical name *it*, there is no requirement for the *it*-designation; thus, because of the paribhāṣā "the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*," there is no fault. Furthermore, in the case of the rule *bhavataṣṭhakchasau*, there is no fault because each [suffix] is taught individually. In examples such as *cokūḥ*, there is no fault because it is a technical name belonging to another system of grammar (*vyākaraṇāntarīya*). And in the rule *lopaśca*, it is assumed that the status of being produced through *praśleṣa* (conjunction) is intended.

In examples such as *ai-u-ṇ*, the designation *it* applies to the entire aggregate because it prescribes the correctness of the phoneme *u* and others; [this is so] because in *citraṅ*, the word *ḍit* is a separate word, and that signifies "having the marker *ḍ*" (*ḍit*). Since the status of being *ṅit* is prescribed in conjunction with *kyac*, there is no fault regarding the requirement for its actual existence; therefore, an instrumentive derivation (*bhāvasādhana*) alone is appropriate. In cases such as *ai-u-ṇ*, there is no status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because the specific aggregate lacks the capacity to convey meaning.

Regarding the statement in the *Manoramā* that "in the rule *lopaśca*, although *śas* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it does not denote [the suffix], because in the enumeration [of items], only those denoting verbal roots and the like are included; thus, there is a fault in taking the word as an instrumental derivative"—this is correctly characterized as a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). This is not so, however, because the faults in cases such as *laṭassadvā*, *niṣṭhā*, *rājasūya*, and *bhavataṣṭhakchasau* have already been firmly established during the occasion of explaining those very rules.

Furthermore, there is the burden of assuming that the technical designation *it* applies solely by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and because the flaw remains inevitable under the view that in rules such as "coḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.52), the vowel *u* bears the designation *it*. There is also the burden of assuming the force of a phonetic combination (*praśleṣa*). Moreover, the capacity of [the sūtras] such as "a i u" (Pāṇini 1.1.1) to prescribe grammatical correctness has already been refuted. And there is the burden of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the verbal root *citraṅ* and of postulating a separate sentence. Finally, the claim that words such as "root" (*dhātu*) occurring in the list of exceptions refer to those specific indicators has already been refuted.

Furthermore, because the author himself has stated that [the section beginning with] *a-i-u-ṇ* possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of its indicating a sequence; and because there is no stronger evidence to suggest that the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). As for the objection raised in the first four instances according to the view of "others" (*anye tu*)—namely, that after removing the fault by treating the rule *lopaś ca* as providing a specific capacity (i.e., making the substitute *ś* a replacement for the whole) such that it was previously unknown, its utterance constitutes "being taught" (*upadiśyamānatva*) as something new—and that the form of *citraṅ* containing its indicatory letter (*anubandha*) was likewise unknown: [this is refuted].

[Objection: But surely, since there is no nasalized (anunāsika) pronunciation in the treatise (śāstra), the knowledge of the true nature [of the phonemes] is difficult to obtain; therefore, he says: "By convention" (pratijñā). The meaning is that they possess nasality which is the object of a convention. The phrase "the Pāṇinīyas" means the phonemes taught by Pāṇini and others. A "convention" (pratijñā) is a statement such as "this is thus," as well as the linguistic usage that makes known the true nature of the phonemes. The sense is that through these two, that knowledge is easily obtained. And because of proximity, those who establish the convention are none other than the authors of that very treatise; this is the general direction. [He says] "from the indication" (nirdeśāt).

The intention is that if those [vowels] were included therein, there would be the undesirable consequence (*yaṇāpatti*) regarding the nose and so forth; however, they say that if [the vowels] are not included, there is no fault in that regard. The followers of the Upādhyāya maintain that this too has been refuted by the present [rule].

"Because of the absence of nasalized pronunciation"—the word "now" (*idānīm*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the meaning is that at present the reading of that [text] has been lost. By this, the sense is that for Asada and others there is an absence of knowledge of that [nasalization]. However, the literal reading is not correct; it is refuted by the fact that there is no restrictive rule stating that Pāṇini and others pronounce only the nasalized [form], and because it would result in redundancy with the term *tattvajñāna* ("knowledge of reality"). [The phrase] "possessing nasality" (*ānunāsikyavantaḥ*).

The sense is that because the form *asuvvata* is used in the Bhāṣya, the rule "not from a *karmadhāraya*" (*na karmadhārayāt*) is merely occasional (*kvācitka*). "This being so" means that in the case of the substitute *aṭ*, the state of having an anusvāra as the penultimate letter (*anunāsikopadhatva*) is established, and so forth. "Usage" refers to [the definition] beginning with "the independent agent is the *kartṛ*. "The contingency of *yaṇ*" [is mentioned].

The point is this: from the word *nāsā*, when the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), the elision of the *ya* sound (by *yasyeti ca*) would apply, as would the shortening of the vowel (by *ke'ṇaḥ*). However, because the rule for shortening (*keṇaḥ*) is an exception (*apavāda*), it applies first. Since there is the possibility that the exception-rule (*apavāda-śāstra*) might become redundant once the general rule (*utsarga*) subsequently applies, the general rule does not apply. Consequently, by the rule *pratyayasthāt...*, the *i* is substituted [for the long *ā*], and since there is still the possibility that the exception-rule might be redundant, the rule *yasyeti ca* does not apply; thus, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs. This is the intended meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the short vowel [substitution] rule (*hrasva*) finds its scope of application (*cāritārthya*) in cases such as *niṣādika-dhūka* and thus cannot be considered an exception (*apavāda*). For even there, since the *guṇa* substitution for the *oḥ* vowels would apply, the short vowel rule lacks scope of application. Furthermore, one should not argue that the general rule (*utsarga-śāstra*), which operates immediately after the operation of the exceptional rule (*apavāda-pravṛtti*), does not apply due to the possibility of the exceptional rule becoming redundant; and thus, if the elision (*lopa*) does not occur after the short vowel, the elision after the *ī* vowel would indeed be unavoidable. This is because [the general rule] does not fail to apply merely on the basis of such a possibility.

Where there is the possibility of the application of a general rule (*utsarga-śāstra*) being rendered purposeless by a specific exception (*apavāda-śāstra*), the general rule does not apply; since this meaning is rooted in the purposelessness of the specific exception, even the anticipation of application at a later time—occurring after an interval—is prevented wherever there is the possibility of the specific exception being purposeless.

Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for assuming the non-application of the elision of *ya* (yasyeti-lopa)—which occurs at a time subsequent to the interval following the application of the shortening rule (*hasva*)—on the grounds that the purpose of the exception (*apavāda*) is fulfilled by the non-application of the *guṇa* rule occurring immediately after the shortening rule in cases such as *naipādaka-dhūka*. This is because, by including the *aṇ*-pratyāhāra, the rule regarding the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would still lack its scope of application (*acāritārthya*) even with that much [exclusion].

Alternatively, according to the direction stated by Śrīdhara—that in the rule *yaci bham*, the term *ac* is understood as being delimited only by the two properties of being a vowel (*actva*) and being a consonant (*haltva*), due to its association with the letter *y*—the elision of *y* (via *yasyeti ca*) would not apply, resulting in the undesirable occurrence of *yaṇ* substitution; this is how it should be understood. By this, the views of the Ācāryas—who maintain that the elision of *y* should be applied here on the grounds of [the stem] being a nominal base (*aṅga*)—as well as the views of the authors of the *Prakāśa* who seek to defend those opinions, are refuted. Nor should it be argued that even if the [elision] is prevented by the aforementioned association (*sāhacarya*), the preceding element would still undergo the *Śākala* primitive form (*prakṛtibhāva*) because it possesses the status of a word (*padatva*).

This is because of the prohibition [of *prakṛtibhāva*] by the rule "not in a compound" (*na samāse*). As for the objection raised by the author of the *Prakāśa*—namely, that the prohibition "not in a compound" does not apply here (as in *paramacakri atra*), since one must resort to the application of that prohibition specifically regarding the first vowel of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) within such a compound in order to ensure *prakṛtibhāva* in examples like *samiacicad*—and his subsequent attempt to ward off *prakṛtibhāva* by interpreting the rule as "at the end of a word" (*pade'nta*), that is incorrect.

Since the prohibition applies only when [the augment] is expressed as a constituent part of that compound, the previously mentioned prohibition does not apply to the aforementioned case; otherwise, the qualification "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*) would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that in *sami-acicat*, there would be an application of the prohibition because *ac* is a constituent of the compound; for since the rule has *aṭ* following a form ending in *caṅ* as its objective, it does not have the compound as its objective, and thus lacks the status of being a constituent of a compound.

It should not be argued that, by the example that "the fetus residing within a pregnant woman is not included by the term 'pregnant woman' itself," the state of being "included therein" means merely having an existence subsequent to the existence of that [container], and thus the presence of the vowel *a* as a constituent of the compound (in *agarbhiṇīstha*)—which is not constituted by the relationship between the subject and the predicate—is unavoidable.

Even so, since you must necessarily state that in the present context the term *aj* lacks the status of being a "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*)—despite its being composed of meaningful words where the subsequent member is established—it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to hold that the prohibition applies precisely to those [words] whose initial constituent is meaningful, rather than assuming that the prohibition is conditioned by the status of being a subsequent member. Thus, by the fitness of the meaning, the prohibition is established in the present case.

Furthermore, since it is simpler to enjoin the status of being a constituent part of the *uttarapada* (the second member of a compound) rather than the status of being a constituent part of the initial element of the *uttarapada*, the prohibition is established in the present case. In the example *sami acicat*, although the status of being a constituent part of the compound is obtained through the principle of "falling in the middle" (*tanmadhyapatita-nyāya*), the status of being a constituent part of the *uttarapada* is not obtained; thus, the prohibition does not apply. The absence of *yaṇ*-substitution is established by the force of the rule itself. This is because it is more appropriate for that [rule] to be the basis for the absence of *yaṇ* only by way of making known that even in *pratyāhāras* (abbreviated vowel series), the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are not included.

This is because this interpretation is more appropriate than assuming a contradiction with the direct teaching (*sākṣāc-chāstra-bādhaka*). The intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the phrase "because of the mention" (*nirdeśāt*) is that it is due to the capacity of the rule (*vidhāna-sāmarthya*) which serves as its source. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as *tṛṣi-mūṣi-kuṣibhyaḥ ekaḥ pūrvaś ca* are included. Now, one might object: "In the case of a pratyāhāra [formed by an indicatory letter], why is there no exclusion of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) when [the term] *ac* is used for the purpose of including vowels?"

Furthermore, regarding the purpose of preventing the fault [of over-extension] there: if one accepts the meaning "at the end of a word" (*pade'nta*) for the sake of avoiding that defect, then such a meaning would have to follow from the governing topic (*adhikāra*) of "meaning" (*artha*) in the subsequent sūtra; however, in the reading already stated, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Now, since the principle of *bāhulaka* (diversity/irregularity) is the resort for those who have no other way out, he says: "by the suffix *ac* in the sense of 'possessing' (*arśa-ādi*). Others, however, say: here, the assumption of its being the beginning of a class (*ādi*) despite its not being listed among them is no different from relying on *bāhulaka*; the only difference is the difficulty involved in postulating two distinct grammatical functions (*vṛtti*). Here, the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *mātrac* should be understood.

Based on the Bhāṣya statement "half-a-short [vowel]," which indicates that the word *ardhahasva* itself signifies the meaning of half a mātrā, he says: "the word *hrasva*. The intention is that in the root text (*mūla*), it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word *ardhahasva* denotes the measure consisting of half a *mātrā*; following that, the suffix *mātrac* has the object of measurement as its meaning. When the elision occurs according to the rule *tasya pramāṇam*, the result is "the part consisting of half a *mātrā*," and this is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. Therefore, he says: "in the form conventionally established by one's own treatise."

The meaning is: "of that which has half a *mātrā* as its duration. Why "half a *mātrā*"? This is an explanation of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) of the suffix *-mātra*; however, it cannot be intended as an explanation of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*). This is because a *mātrā* is a measure (*parimāṇa*), and thus there can be no connection with a property such as "acute" (*udātta*) belonging to it. Precisely because this [term] does not convey meaning through its technical (*saṅketita*) form [in grammar], its inclusion [in the rule] serves a purpose. In the case of the term *svarita*, even in long vowels (*dīrgha*) and so forth, only half a *mātrā* is acute.

Starting from here, prior to the word *a* in the rule *navalūcyā*, this [term] applies even to the Tripādī section by virtue of its extended application (*utkarṣa*). All of this is clear in the Bhāṣya. As for the commentary stating "the first half is acute" (*ardhamudāttaṃ*), it is explained as a metaphorical designation (*vyākhyā*) similar to the expression "Satyabhāmā" (used for Satyabhāmā). And the meaning of "the latter half" (*uttarārdha*) is the subsequent portion remaining after the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*). In the Veda, however, the determination follows the actual usage and this Prātiśākhya. Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*), it means "of the anudātta. Regarding "acute" (*udātta*), etc. [the following applies].

The meaning is: "when they [the acute and circumflex accents] follow. And their following is only in relation to the preceding *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel. "Elsewhere" means: in the absence of the acute and circumflex accents following. "In the Prātiśākhya" implies that in common usage (*loka*), however, it is only *anudātta*. He provides an example of a short *svarita*: *keti*. In *kim oditi*, by the rule "kāti," there is the substitution of *kā*; then, by the rule "titsvaritam," it becomes *svarita*. He provides an example of a long [circumflex]: *rathānām iti*. *yerā iti*.

The vowel *e* is svarita by the rule "svarito vā anudātte padādau"; however, the prohibition "nodāttasvaritodayam" applies only to that which immediately follows [the rule] "udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ".

Since the desired result could have been achieved simply by changing the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [to the first], that [genitive form] is used for the purpose of including the long and *svarita* vowels. For in the case of the long vowels and so on which serve as indicators (*bodhaka*) according to the technical terminology of the science (*śāstra*), the presence of a short vowel is impossible; thus, its [the genitive’s] lack of applicability there is quite evident. Now, one might object: "But since the *svarita* vowels produced by the *ādeśa* rules (e.g., *ādyudāttaśca*) are considered *asiddha*, this rule would not apply to them, and consequently, the inclusion of those [long *svaritas*] would be impossible. Therefore, the use of the genitive is meaningful for the sake of including them. To this, he says: "From here onwards," and so forth.

The intention is that, since [the fault of] being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) does not apply in this way, the word "that" (*tat*) is not for the purpose of including that [case]. Regarding the phrase "before *a a*": although in the Bhāṣya an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) is seen after the rule "an udātta followed by an anudātta becomes svarita," nevertheless, with the view that in the rule "not [before] an udātta or svarita followed by... (*nodāttasvaritodayam*), the Bhāṣya intends either a remote posteriority (*vyavahitaparatva*) or a posteriority relative to that specific sūtra in order to obtain the object of the prohibition, it was stated thus. And the evidence (*jñāpaka*) for such an upward displacement is the sūtra "anudāttau suppitau" (P. 3.1.4), which prescribes anudātta for the case endings (*sup*) and gerund suffixes (*pit*).

Otherwise, in the case of *anyathā devā brahmāṇaḥ*, when the rule "an udātta following an udātta becomes svarita" (*udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*) is to be applied, that [subsequent rule] would be invalid (*asiddha*); thus, its inconsistency [with the observed form] would be quite evident. The benefits of this [interpretation] regarding excellence are to be understood from the source (the *Ākara*). He dispels the contradiction with the observed forms (*lakṣya*) by stating "in the Veda."

[This is] by way of logic (*nyāya*) in the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara* accompanied by the grace of the Guru. He cites an example where a *svarita* follows: *śatacakram*. [The form] *ahyaḥ* has the sense of *aheḥ*; it means "of Vṛtra. There is an absence of *guṇa* substitution due to the rule: "In the Veda, there is optionally the statement [of non-substitution] prior to the suffix *ṇau* and *caṅ* with respect to the penultimate vowel. The *svarita* arises from the rule *udāttasvaritayor...* (P. 8.2.4). But [the application of] *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* (P. 6.1.174) does not apply because it is Vedic. The word *yat* is *antodātta* by the rule *phiṣaḥ* (P. 1.1.43), and its single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is optionally *svarita*. As for *saḥ*:
the meaning is that it is designated as having an acute accent (*udātta*), a short vowel (*hrasva*), and so forth.

"Face" (*mukha*) is called "speech" (*vacana*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*) by virtue of the rule of general application (*bāhulaka*). Thus, the meaning is "the speech of the face. As for the root *ah* [in the word *ahi*], it means "to pervade" (*vyāpti*). Although one might derive [the form] from this root with the suffix *yat*, such a derivation is to be disregarded because it belongs to the Vedic language (*chāndasa*), because the substitution of *dhy* would not apply, and because it would result in a lack of semantic connection and contradict the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "of the acute and circumflex" (*udāttasvaritayoḥ*): since the word *ahi* belongs to the *uñchādi* group, its final syllable is acutely accented; the point is that the *yaṇ*-substitute [for the vowel *i*] takes the place of an acute accent.

Regarding the statement "like a snake with its coils" (*ahiriva bhogaiḥ*), the author of the *Prakāśa* maintains that since the initial vowel is heard as udātta, it must be udātta either by virtue of belonging to the *grāma* group or the *vṛṣa* group; consequently, the following *ī* becomes anudātta due to the rule of *śeṣanighāta*. Then, by the rule "after an udātta, an anudātta becomes svarita," the *ī* becomes svarita, and because the *yaṇ* substitute takes its place, the resulting *yaṇ* is also established as svarita. This is his view. However, that is not correct.

Because the rules *udāttādanudāttasya* and *udāttasvaritayoḥ* would be productive [of accent] in those cases, the *śeṣanighāta* (the rule for the remaining syllables) would not apply; consequently, it would be difficult to establish the anudātta nature of the initial *a*, and thus the option *svarito vā* could not be applied, resulting in the failure to produce svarita for the *y* and *u*. Furthermore, this would lead to a lack of consistency with the subsequent text beginning with *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*.

By this, the statement of the author of the *Prakāśa*—who, taking the word "svarita" from the rule *etena vā svaritaḥ*, asserts that the meaning is that the single substitute for a *svarita* followed by a remaining *anudātta* (by the rule *svaritovānudātte padādau*) is *svarita* when it occurs between an *udātta* and a *svarita*—is refuted. You should understand that the proof for its inclusion in the *uñchādi* group is simply the fact that the vowel *o* in the present example is heard as *svarita*.

"Regarding the suffix *lyuṭ* [in the word *vacana*], it is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). This is according to the *Vṛtti*. In the *Bhāṣya*, however, the term *vacana* ending in *lyuṭ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is shown to be a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Although a *tatpuruṣa* is simpler than a *bahuvrīhi*, nevertheless, due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), and because the *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object is a "resort of last resort" (*agatikagati*), the *bahuvrīhi* alone is superior. For this very reason, the Bhaṭṭas, having stated that this is according to the *Vṛtti*, have shown the *bahuvrīhi* itself as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "In the *Bhāṣya*, however," and so forth. By this, those who claim that there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in taking the *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object are refuted.

Furthermore, the analysis [of the compound] is not "the nose (*nāsikā*) together with *ḍīp*, *sya*, and so forth," where the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Rather, it is a *kṛt*-based compound meaning "that by which speech is produced" (*tayā vacanam*), as stated in the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā*. Thus he says: "together with the mouth," and so on. Why include the word "mouth" (*mukha*)? Otherwise, [the designation *anunāsika*] would apply only to the *yama*s and the *anusvāra*s. And in that case, the *anusvāra* would be subject to the rule *aṅo 'nunāsikaḥ*. Why include the word "nose" (*nāsikā*)? So that in words such as *śakti*, the elision of *k* by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* etc., might not occur. [The number] eighteen, and so forth.

Although this [compound] is not possible in the case of a cross-division (*vyatipakṣe*) because individuals are infinite, nevertheless, the meaning is that [the compound] refers to things such as the genus *akāra* (the letter 'a') which possess eighteen properties. This must be stated. There is no fault, however, because a compound is accepted with a neuter-ending word when it denotes a universal (*sāmānya*). And this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. Or, the compound is like *kukkuṭāṇḍa* ("a hen's egg"). Thus, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the nose with the mouth as its second" (*mukhadvitīyā nāsikā*); that is to say, the analysis has that meaning.

Since it will be stated later that the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) serves to exclude examples such as *śākapriyapārthiva*, this elision is established as obligatory; consequently, the reading "with the nose together with the mouth" (*mukhasahitanāsikayā*) would result in a lack of consistency with the root text (*mūla*). Therefore, the literal reading is not correct. It should be understood, however, that the presentation of the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) for that purpose is intended to demonstrate that the word *dvitīya* mentioned in the Bhāṣya expresses "conjunction" (*sāhitya*). [The rule] "the instrument is expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix" (*sādhanaṃ kṛtā*)...

Although this [formation] is established here even by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), it has been stated in this way specifically to indicate that a Vārttika is necessary for the purpose of compounding in the case of *pādahāraka*, where the word ending in the fifth case (*apādāna*) must be compounded. "It should be an *anusvāra*" means it should be the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*). The point is that, because the technical name *yama* is etymologically significant—meaning "that which restrains"—and because one observes that these [sounds] do not undergo elision (*lopa*), they lack the status of being substitutes (*ādeśa*) and thus do not possess a genitive case relation (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) [to a specific original sound]; therefore, there is no possibility of their application. This is according to the method of the Sūtra.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the mention of "mukha" (mouth) is rejected on the analogy of the "residents of the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*). Regarding the word *śaktā*: this is a form ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* attached to a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle). There is also a reading *śaktaḥ* found in some places. Now, an objection is raised: since in the root text only the short vowels *i* and *u* are mentioned, and since these represent only a single individual (*vyakti*), it is inconsistent to speak of eighteen varieties for them. However, if they were intended as representations (*anukaraṇa*) of the actual phonetic instances found in usage (*lakṣya*), then because those instances are infinite, the number eighteen would remain inconsistent.

Under the view that [phonemes] are individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), since it is an imitation of a short vowel, even the properties residing therein would not number eighteen; with this intention, he raises an objection, beginning with "Even though... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to infinity" (*ānantyāt*): this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It implies that the individualities (*tadvyaktitva*) residing therein are likewise infinite, and that there are six [qualities], such as the acute accent (*udāttatva*) and so on. [The opponent objects: "But even under the view that [phonemes] are universals (*jātipakṣa*), since the universal is one, how [can there be eighteen] given the infinity of the individuals that serve as its substrata?"

This should be understood by relying on the distinction between shortness (*isvatva*) and so forth, as well as the acute (*udātta*) and nasalized (*anunāsika*) qualities that are co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with them; the same applies hereafter. Regarding the phrase "of the *la*-vowel": this means "of the *la*-vowel in its wide-open (*vivṛta*) state. By this, there is no contradiction even if the long vowel (*dīrgha*)—which is to be prescribed by the rule "in place of *l*, *la* or *v*" (*lati lavā*)—is slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). This is because there is an absence of a long [nasalized] vowel. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the *Tulyāsyaprayatna* sūtra, it says: "In order to establish the inclusion of eighteen [varieties] for the *la*-vowel, he says: 'Possession of the eighteen properties.'"

The sense is that, in the view that [the word] denotes the universal (*jāti*), when the substrata of universals such as *a*-ness and so forth are presented, their possession of the eighteen properties remains unimpeded. Bringing this out, he says: "The meaning is 'of those belonging to the class of the letter *a*, etc. By this, the following must be considered: even in the view that it denotes the universal, although all individual instances are made the objects of a single cognition by virtue of that universal, infinity remains unavoidable; therefore, even in that view, one must state that the properties themselves are eighteen in number.

Thus, even the passage beginning with "tathāpi" (nevertheless) is indeed inconsistent if it intends the theory of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*). For in that view, since the property of being that specific individual (*tadvyaktitva*) alone would be the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and since the property of being pervaded by that (*tadvyāpyatva*) does not exist in the eighteen [possible] properties, a classification—which consists in making known all the mutually contradictory properties pervaded by [the denotable capacity]—is impossible. Nor can this be justified by [claiming] the property of being one of the many [individuals] (*nānātadvyaktitvānyatamatva*) as the pervader; for, due to the infinity of individuals, it is impossible to grasp all those individualities.

Therefore, the mention of "the position of individuals" (*vyaktipakṣa*) is merely an illustration; it includes the "position of universals" (*jātipakṣa*) as well. Thus, the statement of the author of the *Ākāśakṛt* is refuted. Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated above that mutual contradiction does not apply to the divisions [of accents]. Now, one might ask: "Are not properties (*dharma*) also of exactly eight kinds? To this he replies: "Of shortness, etc. This means: in relation to the acute accent (*udātta*) residing in the same substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as itself. Although in the world it is observed that only non-artificial (natural) cognition possesses the power to induce activity or cessation, nevertheless, here, by virtue of the authority of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), even an artificial superimposition (*āhāryāropa*) is to be understood as the regulator of the operation or non-operation of the treatise. In this context, if the effect were *asiddha*, there would be the failure of forms such as *amū*.

When the form *ada a au* is established, although the substitution of *m* (mutva) takes precedence due to its later position in the order of rules, and although that [substitution] is considered "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*) from the perspective of the operations contained within the first seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*), there is no occurrence of the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) or others because of the absence of the vowel *a*, according to the maxim of "the killer of Devadatta being killed himself" (*devadattahantṛhatanyāya*). This is because, since an extension (*atideśa*) consists of a superimposition (*āropa*), a superimposition without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna*) is impossible; therefore, on this view, the application of the grammatical operation is necessary.

Regarding its non-establishment by the technical rules (*śāstra-asiddhatva*): even in cases where a rule belonging to the tripādī section has already applied due to its being *antaraṅga*, there too—by means of the superimposition of non-existence upon that very rule—there is an absence of the cognition of its cessation, an absence of the cognition of a substitute (*ādeśa*), and an absence of the cognition that [the operation] has occurred in the target form (*lakṣya*). However, the operation that is actually taking place proceeds with respect to the substitute itself through the cognition of it as the original base (*sthānin*). There is no fault here, for the activity prompted by the delusion of silver does not fail to have mother-of-pearl as its object.

But where there is a simultaneous application (*sahaprasaṅga*), the particle *api* alone [indicates non-application], because of the superimposition of non-existence (*abhāvāropa*). Nor should it be argued that in the previous case the rule should simply be "na" (negation); for if the meaning were "negation when a preceding rule would otherwise apply," then the rule *nalopaḥ supi* would be inconsistent, since that rule is intended as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*). According to your view, in the stage "rājan-aśva," since no preceding rule applies at all, this negation would not operate; thus, once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has occurred, this [subsequent] rule would not apply by the maxim of "one who has already eaten" (*bhuktavantaḥ*), resulting in the form "rājāśve."

Because the rule of lengthening (*dīrgha*) would render the restriction (*niyama*) useless; and because [if that were the case], lengthening would undesirably apply even in examples such as *rājabhyām*. Furthermore, if the meaning [of the rule] were "when there is the possibility of the scope of a preceding rule," then in cases like *rājabhyām*, since there is a possibility of the scope of the *sub*-rule (for the *bhyām* ending) and the rule for lengthening, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would never occur. This is the general direction of the argument. Regarding "external effort" (*bāhyaprayatna*): these [efforts] function to produce effects consisting of the expansion and contraction of the glottis below the larynx (*kākalaka*), the production of breath, specific sounds (*nāda*), specific qualities of that sound such as resonance (*ghoṣa*) and non-resonance (*alpaghoṣa*), and the smallness or greatness of the vital air (*prāṇa*). To explain: [The text continues with a list of these external efforts.]
The self, having come into contact with objects through the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the bodily fire, which impels the vital air.
"The vital air (māruta), having been impelled and struck at the head, takes a curved path and produces the phonemes"—thus it is stated in the *Śikṣā*.

The "Self" (ātman) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Having brought together, through its own activity, the objects residing within itself in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), and having made them the object of a single cognition, it joins the mind (*manas*) with the desire to manifest them. That mind, possessing such a desire, strikes the fire of the body—the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). That bodily fire, being struck, impels that vital air upward; such is the meaning of the passage beginning with "impelled" (*sodīrṇaḥ*).

And thus, air impelled from the region of the navel by fire struck by the effort produced by the desire to employ speech, having traveled with speed as far as the head and then returned, reaches the mouth; aided by the aforementioned effort, it strikes the various places of articulation—beginning with contact by the tip of the tongue—and manifests the phonemes. Thereafter, by means of specific efforts, it effects the opening of the glottis and other such actions.

In this context, those efforts which strike various specific locations are called "internal" (*ābhyantara*) because they produce their respective effects within the mouth. Those that cause the expansion of the glottis and so forth are called "external" (*bāhya*) because they produce their effects in a location outside the mouth. As for shortness (*hrasvatva*) and other qualities such as being measured by a *mātrā*, these are caused by the smallness or greatness of the air; thus, a certain distinct effort from the region of the navel impels a small amount of air while another impels a greater amount. Since the effect consisting of the impelling of that air occurs in a location outside the mouth, that too is indeed external.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *aiuṇ* sūtra: "The mention of *aṇ* in the *savarṇa* sūtra is due to the fact that the effort (*yatna*) which produces shortness and so forth is a qualifier of the mouth (*āsya*). Although it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ* sūtra that "there is indeed a single effort which produces all effects and also destroys the phonemes," nevertheless, one should understand that such usage occurs by superimposing a distinction upon what is actually one, based on the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of its respective effect.

Although the effort that produces [qualities] such as the acute accent (*udātta*) performs an internal operation, those [efforts] which are understood even without the words "acute" and so forth—because their non-intentionality is indicated by the rule *anaṅ udāttaḥ* and because they are not utilized for the technical designation of homogeneity (*savarṇa-saṃjñā*)—are nonetheless counted among the external [articulatory efforts] due to a similarity consisting in their utility for the examination of "nearness" (*antara-tamya*). This [point] is an illustration for [the inclusion of] shortness (*hrasvatva*) and so forth, as well as nasality (*ānunāsikya*).

Regarding "śara": [the letters] ś, ṣ, s, and h. "Anupradāna" refers to the external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*). Regarding "they open up" (*vivṛṇvate*): one should understand that this expresses the agency of these [sounds] in the dilation of the glottis (*kaṇṭhavivara*) which occurs subsequent to their manifestation. The sense is that *vivāra* (opening) is their effort. Regarding "others, however": this means the third, fourth, and fifth letters of each *varga*, as well as their corresponding *yamas*, the letter *ha*, the *anusvāra*, and the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*.

"Those possessing the *nāda* [quality]" means those produced with that effort. Although in the case of the *khay*-class and others, the requirements of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) are fulfilled by the mere effort of either voiced (*ghoṣa*) or voiceless (*aghoṣa*), nevertheless, the statement regarding the others is made in accordance with the *Śikṣā* treatises. "Having little breath" means having little vital air (*alpaprāṇa*), because after the utterance of these, there is as it were a diminution of the vital airs. Regarding the phrase "in the classes" (*vargeṣu*), the words "of those that exist" (*vidyamānānām*) are to be supplied. "Of four"—[refers to each class].

The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), with the word "one of them" (*anyatama*) understood as the remainder. Regarding the phrase "similar to the preceding": this similarity is produced by effort. For this very reason, the inclusion of the *yamas* among the *ayogavāhas* is consistent both with the statement in the Bhāṣya, "And four *yamas* are recorded," and with Pāṇini’s *Śikṣā*, "The *yamas* are remembered as four. And he says that this [similarity] occurs only in the Veda, citing the *Prātiśākhya*. Regarding the phrase "of others": the meaning is "of the vowels" (*acām*) and "of the previously mentioned non-consonants" (*uktānyahālām*). In the phrase "and *ya-ra-la-va*," the word "and" (*ca*) includes the vowels as well.

According to the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *supāṃ suluk*—"the letter *d* [is substituted] for the letter *i* due to internal similarity (*antaryataḥ*)"—vowels (*ac*) possess voicedness (*ghoṣatva*), closure (*saṃvāra*), sonority (*nāda*), and weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇatva*). Otherwise, in the case of *tad-au*, the two [substitutes *tau* and *dau*] would alternate; if weak aspiration were not admitted, then in the case of *dadhi-au*, the two [substitutes *dadhau* and *dadhau*] would alternate. The voicedness of vowels is also clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*. The phrase "others" means: the second and fourth [consonants], their corresponding semivowels (*yamau*), the letters *ś, ṣ, s, h*, and the *ayogavāha*s.

The mention of the place of articulation (*sthāna*) and external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*) for the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *yamās*, and so forth, is for the purpose of determining their specific nature (*svarūpa-nirṇaya*).

However, it should be understood that this [homogeneity] is not useful for the examination of internal proximity (*āntaratamya*) and so forth. The phrase "they are not useful" is because the word *pra* is included in the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (P. 1.1.9). For if they were useful, there would be homogeneity even between *ś* and *ch*; such is the intention. Furthermore, the examination of internal proximity will become clear in various places through statements such as "of those possessing resonance" (*ghoṣavataḥ*). "Contact consonants" (*sparśāḥ*) are those designated by that term. The word *antasthā* ends in a vowel. Its meaning is: they stand within, in the middle, between the contact consonants (*sparśa*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
