"Ūṣman" means wind; the sense is that they have that [wind] as their primary constituent. Thus, it is clearly stated in the *Prātiśākhya-bhāṣya* that the meaning of "sopmāṇaḥ" is "those which exist together with wind. Although, according to the commentary on the rule *sthānentaratamaḥ*, the quality of being an *ūṣman* also belongs to the second and fourth letters of the classes [the sibilants and h], nevertheless, only these [the first and third of each class] are understood in the rule *vivṛtamūṣmaṇām*. The point is that otherwise, since the guttural and other sounds would share the same place of articulation (*sthāna*), the grammatical rules such as *nājjhalau* would become inconsistent. "Vowels (*ac*) are the *svaras* (sounds)."

Because of the etymological derivation that they "shine by themselves" through [the qualities of] acute (*udātta*) and so forth, the acute and other accents are also called *svaras* (sounds), since they possess those properties. In the phrase "by *ka* and *pa*," this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *kha* and *pha*. The mention of *aṃ* and *aḥ* is likewise an elliptical indication for *i*, *u*, and the others. Thus he says: "following a vowel. Regarding the phrase "of the *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds": the analysis is "the *ṛ* sound and the *ḷ* sound"; there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*. It is precisely for this purpose that the letter *ḷ* is included in the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*); otherwise, due to the doubt that it might not be a real entity (*asattva*), even this very statement would be subject to doubt.

This has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *eoṅiti*. For there, in examples such as *saṃyantā*, it is raised as an objection that since the letters *ya* and others—which have a duration of one *mātrā*—are included among the components of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) by the rule *halonantarāḥ* when viewed through the lens of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the teaching on the inclusion of letters), a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) dependent upon a consonant (*vyañjana*) would not apply. In response, it is stated that because consonants of one *mātrā* are not taught [as independent phonemes], and because that which is not taught does not exist, and because it is impossible to apprehend what is non-existent, those [consonants] are not grasped by the rule *aṇudit-sūtra*.

Nor does the absence of *pluta* (protracted) lengthening follow from the prohibition "not in the case of falsehood" (*anṛte*) in rules such as *na ca klṛptaśikha*; for there is no fault, since *ṛ* and *ḷ* are treated as separate *anubandhas*, and it is possible to assume that in certain instances they do not mutually include one another due to their distinct *la*-status.

Regarding the phrase "of the letters *a* and *ha*": according to the view that the letter *e* is palatal (*tālavya*) and the letter *o* is labial (*auṣṭhya*), this [rule] is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the letters *e*, *ś*, and so forth. By this, the objection that it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as "*anāścalau*" is refuted. Since the result would be established by the rule "*haśi ca*" alone, the mention of "*atoror*" is for the purpose of excluding the vowel *ā*. He demonstrates a *madhyamapadalopisamāsa* (middle-term-omitted compound) in order to justify the dual number in the sūtra.

"Accompanied by the vowel *ā*" (*ākārasahita*): for this very reason, the designation "in the case of the vowels [velāsu]" is justified. However, if it were a collective *dvandva* compound, there would be the undesirable application of the suffix *ṭac*; moreover, having formed a collective *dvandva* according to the rule *ajjhalau*, if it were then a *dvandva* with the word *ā*, the *ā*-vowel would not share the same place of articulation (*sāvarṇya*) even with the vowels beginning with *a*. This is the intended meaning. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* establishes the absence of *sāvarṇya* among these [vowels] due to the difference in their effort (*prayatna*). Regarding the phrase "when these follow": this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood to mean "of that which exists when these are present. By this, the inclusion of long vowels and so forth is secured when *ha* and other consonants follow *a* and other vowels.

"It would be *ac-ness*" means "it would be the state of being understood by the term *ac*. This is to be understood according to the view that the application of the defining rule (*grāhaka-śāstra*) extends even to the constituent elements of the *pratyāhāra*, and according to the theory of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*).

*Anu-di*: With reference to *aṇ*, the status of being a denoter of its own class (*savarṇa*) is here enjoined. The word "denoter" (*bodhakaḥ*) is to be supplied as the complement to "of its own class" (*savarṇa*). He says this in order to exclude the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*) in the case of substitutes (*ādeśa*) and so forth.

Regarding the term *pratīyate*: others, however, argue that by accepting [the word] *pratyaya* as a partial concession (*ekadeśānumati*), it correctly serves to indicate the *paribhāṣā* rule: "That which is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include [the inclusion of] homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). Yet, it is not correct to take the word *pratyaya* as having that specific meaning [of the *paribhāṣā*], because the author of the Vārttika provides a supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the rules concerning *ṭit*, *kit*, *mit*, and *nit* suffixes; and because the author of the Bhāṣya states that the mention of *apratyaya* (non-suffix) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this very *paribhāṣā*. This point is also suggested (*dhvanita*) in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *jyādādīyasaḥ*.

In that case, why is "āditya" stated? One might as well say simply "jyād-". What is the grammatical derivation (*rūpasiddhi*)? [One might argue: "By proximity (*āntarya*), a long vowel will be substituted for a long vowel. If this is so, then this very rule indicates the existence of the *paribhāṣā*: "That which is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*)," and so forth. For if one follows the explanation you have provided, both the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) would be rendered groundless. Even under the theory of universals (*jātipakṣa*), the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) must be prevented by this very *paribhāṣā*.

In the view that [the *it* designation] applies to individual letters (*vyaktipakṣa*), the fact that a vowel would not be distinguished from its qualities (*guṇa*) must also be prevented. Consequently, in examples such as *ghaṭavat*, the letter *v* does not become nasalized (*anunāsika*). By this, they say that the objection—that since the rule could have been established simply by saying *ajudi* (without *ṇ*), the inclusion of *ṇ* implies that in the case of *yaṇ* vowels, the qualities do distinguish the letters—is refuted. Now, one might ask: "In forms such as *cori* (from *cur + i*), how can the letter *i* be designated as having the *udic* property, given that it is part of a derivative form (*anuvāda*)? If you say this, we reply: there is no fault, because in other grammatical systems these [letters] are designated as *udic*. Furthermore, since the word *upadeśa* (instruction) functions as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), it refers to the grammatical treatise itself; thus, because this [treatise] is indeed a *śāstra*, the application of the *it* designation is easily established. He says that the particle *ca* ("and") is placed out of its logical order.

Regarding the term *udicca*: although phonemes that are homogenous (*savarṇa*) with the entire composite [vowel] are not well-known, nevertheless, in this context, those phonemes that are homogenous with the initial elements (*ca*-class) of those composites should be understood as being its constituent sounds. Furthermore, even for the short *a* and so forth, it is easily established that they possess a common place of articulation (*tulyasthānatva*) by superimposing a distinction in their places of articulation based on differences in limiting conditions (*upādhi*), such as time and person.

Regarding this: the meaning is "in the *grāhaka*-sūtra itself," for that is the intention [of the author] based on the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). However, the argument that [the rule] "after a prefix, before *ṛ*" (*upasargād ṛti*) and so forth is due to the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*) is not tenable; for its purpose is already served by the inclusion of the *lṛ* vowel. Similarly, in the case of *iṇ*, it refers only to the subsequent [vowel]. This is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *laṇ*-sūtra, where it is stated that although "before a vowel" (*aci*) would have sufficed in the rule "before *iṇ*" (*iṇ-koḥ*), the heavy designation "before *y* or *v*" (*yv-or*) and the commentary [indicate otherwise]. [Objection: If this is so, then in rules such as "for this [root], before *cvau*" (*asya cvau*), the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*) would not apply.

If it is argued that—since the mention of "a" (in the rule *aṇ*) refers only to those sounds situated in the traditional alphabet (*varṇasamāmnāya*), and since the recognition of those [sounds] occurs through the sign of the letter *ṇ* in a *pratyāhāra*, and since the purpose of the rule is fulfilled when those [sounds] are grasped as non-different from what was uttered among those present at the beginning of the series—it would follow that under the theory of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), because there is a difference between the individual sound there [in the *samāmnāya*] and the individual sound here [in the *sūtra*], the rule would not apply because only what is actually uttered can be the grasper (*grāhaka*) of the second letter and so on within the *pratyāhāra*—this is not so; for there is no fault, as one may resort to the theory of universals (*jātipakṣa*).

For this very reason, the status of being a *jhal* (consonant) and so forth is established for the multiple occurrences of *takāra* and other letters. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *iṇ* in the rule (*sūtra*) need not be made. By the principle "there is homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*," their common class membership (*samānajātitva*) is extended [to the *ḷ* sound as well]; thus, there is no fault in cases such as *upasargād ṛti*. Since common class membership exists for homogeneous sounds other than these [specifically mentioned], and because separate indicatory markers (*anubandha*) are employed, there is no confusion of grammatical operations triggered by the markers *ṛt* and *ḷt*.

In this view, according to the method of the Bhāṣya stated in the remainder of the *aiuṇ* sūtra, just as the rule *taparaḥ* restricts the inclusion of all homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) that would otherwise be obtained through the inclusion of the genus (*jāti*), so too the rule *apratyayaḥ*—by means of a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)—prohibits the inclusion of such homogeneous sounds that would otherwise be obtained. Consequently, there is no fault in rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ*. Likewise, it should be understood that this [rule] also prohibits the inclusion of homogeneous sounds that would otherwise be obtained through the principle that qualities do not differentiate [the genus]. For this very reason, in forms such as *ghaṭavat*, the letter *v* in the suffix *matup* is not nasalized.

Regarding the phrase "by implication": it will be stated that in rules such as "eco 'yavāyāvaḥ," the desired result is achieved by the rule *sthāne 'ntaratama* (P. 1.1.50) alone. In the rule *na yvābhyām*, the vowels *ai* and *au* should be recited in their own forms (*svarūpeṇa*). Likewise, in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*, one should read simply *eṅ*. This is because, in the view that holds there is a mutual designation (*savarṇasañjñā*) among similar sounds, all four [vowels] are included in the rule for *guṇa*.

By the presentation of this [present] sūtra’s lack of purpose, one should understand that it includes both the lack of purpose for employing the two *pratyāhāra*s in the rule defining the technical terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, as well as the lack of purpose for employing them in the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam*. Furthermore, the previously mentioned fact that these two [sounds] do not share the same phonetic quality (*asāvarṇya*) even due to a difference in effort (*prayatna*) must not be forgotten.

The phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*) refers to the view that [phonemes] are individuals (*vyakti*). The meaning is as follows: first there is the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the phonemes; after the instruction, the technical name *it* is established; after that, the formation of abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*) by means of the rule "the beginning with the last" (*ādirantyena*); after that, the technical name *savarṇa*; and after that, the technical names *aṇ*, *u*, and *it*. By this entire collection of sentences, the inclusion of homogeneous phonemes (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*) occurs elsewhere, but here [in the case of *i* and *ś*], the vowel *i* does not include the consonant *ś*. This is based on the principle of the non-completion of a statement (*vākya-aparisamāpti-nyāya*) as stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *na jhalau*.

The intended meaning is as follows: Once the formation of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) is established by the rule *ādirantyena*, and once the meaning of the sentence *na-aj-jhal-au* has been understood, there arises a determination of the scope of this [rule] by excluding its specific domain. Only then, upon the ascertainment of what is to be designated by the term *savarṇa*, can the rule *aṇ-udit-sūtra* be made to convey the inclusion of that many [sounds]. Otherwise, due to the possibility of sublation (*bādhaka*), there would arise a doubt regarding the validity of the grasp of the linguistic capacity (*śaktigraha*) produced by the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam*; consequently, the cognition generated by the *aṇ-udit* rule would not occur. Nor can it be argued that such ascertainment occurs prior to the comprehension of the meaning of this [sentence].

Regarding the term *hoḍha*: since the letter *ha* includes the letter *ā*, this [term] is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of everything that would otherwise apply [to it]. Now, one might object: "Since the *yaṇ* substitutes and their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) are not established, the inclusion of *aṇ* is redundant because the desired result is already achieved by the mention of *ac* alone. To this, he says:

Regarding *yavalāḥ*: because the *Śikṣā* states, "The nasalized [vowels] are not *hrasva*," the term *yaṇ* is not mentioned here. Consequently, in forms such as *saṃyyanta*, the doubling (*dvitva*) of the nasalized *ya*, *va*, or *la*—which have been produced by *parasavarṇa*—is established by the rule *anaci ca*. However, the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by *halo yamām* is optional. Here, this should be understood: since the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) is the referent (*padārtha*) and the *guṇas* (articulatory properties) are the differentiators, the mention of *yaṇ* in this sūtra is intended to include [all its instances].

Therefore, regarding forms such as *bhisaḥ*, he states that because of the inclusion of the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with the *p*) marker and because of the two explanations of the mention of specific phonemes (*varṇa-grahaṇa*) in the sūtra *sahivahoḥ*, the term *tapara* refers to both a *bahuvrīhi* compound and a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa*.

By the words "taḥ paraḥ" (P. 1.1.70) and so forth: when a vowel is being mentioned [as a technical name], by the force of that rule, there is an understanding of all vowels delimited by the letter *a*; thus, the application of the *tapara* rule (P. 1.1.70) does not occur. The first example is "ato bhisa ais" (P. 7.1.9), and the last example is "vṛddhir ādaij" (P. 1.1.1). Although in these cases the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is followed by *t* (i.e., *tapa*), and neither something of equal duration nor its homogeneous counterpart (*savarṇa*) is well-known [in the case of *aij*], nevertheless, because of the employment of *tapara* and the authority of the Bhāṣya, there is no fault, as the meaning is that a vowel understood from a word followed by *t* causes the inclusion of those [vowels] of its own duration.

And this [rule] is for the sake of the designation *it* (the marker *it*), because the mention of *aṇ* does not recur [from the previous rule]. Since qualities (*guṇas*) are differentiators, even though [this rule] is an injunction regarding non-*aṇ* sounds, it sublates the rule *aṇudit* by virtue of its higher status in cases such as *ato bhisa ais*, whereas the present rule finds scope in the portion consisting of the vowel *ā* in examples like *vṛddhir ādaic*. This is because a conflict exists here, given that linguistic usage based on number is observed to function through mutual exclusion. However, it should be understood that if qualities were non-differentiators, there would be no scope [for the former rule], and thus the sublation would not occur.

In this context, although the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applies only to a phoneme (*varṇa*) due to the homogeneity (*sājātya*) between the limit (*avadhi*) and that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*), it should be understood that the production of case-endings (*vibhakti*) occurs from a qualified [term], because it is based on a Vedic rule (*sautratvāt*). Regarding the phrase "of its duration" (*tatkālasya*), its meaning is "of that which has a duration equal to the time of its utterance"; thus he says:

The phrase "only at the same time" (*samakālasyaiva*) contains the particle *eva*, which serves to restate the relationship between the sublated (*bādhyā*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*) as established by logic; this is the intended meaning. However, in the view that [the vowel] is a class (*jāti*), it serves specifically as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), because the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) continues to apply. Likewise, even under the Siddhānta position accepted in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "vṛddhir ādaic," namely that "qualities do not cause differentiation" (*guṇānām abhedakatva*), it serves specifically as a restrictive rule. This [rule] does not apply to the letter *t* of the case-ending in rules such as "ādguṇaḥ," because of the inclusion of the *t* with a following *ṛ* (*taparakaraṇa*) in the rule "upasargād ṛti."

In rules such as *ṛdorap*, there is no fault because [the letter] is indeed the letter *d*. And that [letter *d*], like the letter *t* [in the rule *taparaḥ*], serves either for ease of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) or for ease of articulation (*mukhasukhārtha*), provided there is no compound with the fifth case (*pañcamīsamāsa*). However, according to the view that includes the elision of the letter *d* (*dakārapraśleṣa*) in the rule *taparaḥ*, it should be understood that the letter *d* is the substitute for the place [of articulation] of the letter *dh* and so forth.

The expression "vṛddhir āt" consists of three words—"vṛddhiḥ," "āt," and "aij"—therefore there is no suspicion of the application of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) or the like. The inclusion of the *tapara* marker (the short *a*) is for the sake of removing ambiguity, serving the purpose of the preceding [rule]. In the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra, it is stated that because the non-differentiation of vowels (*guṇas*) is accepted based on an indicator (*jñāpaka*), this [marker] does not serve the purpose of including homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). Furthermore, it serves the purpose of the subsequent [rule] to exclude those with three morae (*trimātra*), as in examples such as *kṛṣṇautkaṇṭhyam* and *gaṅgaughaḥ*. Here, the word *vṛddhi* refers to the word-form itself (*padapara*), since its reference to the meaning (*arthaparatva*) is impossible.

The meaning of the sentence is that *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are non-different from the term "vṛddhi," because identity (*tādātmya*) between a word and its referent is accepted. This is because the cognition of their non-difference in such instances as "The two-syllabled name 'Rāma' is the shatterer of the pride of the wielder of the Pināka bow" is established by experience; this is explained in detail elsewhere. As for the fact that the word *vṛddhi* functions as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it follows from the traditional commentary. Furthermore, although it is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its placement at the beginning of the sūtra is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

In passages such as *apṛkta ekāl* ("an uncombined [suffix] consists of a single phoneme"), the reason for placing the rule to be enjoined first is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya: it is to prevent the misconception that its usage might be incorrect. Although all words denote all meanings, a word generates cognition only when its denotative power (*vācakatva*) has been grasped; therefore, technical rules (*saṃjñā-sūtra*) function as injunctions (*vidhi*) because they make known a power that was previously unknown. Furthermore, the acceptance that "all [words] denote all meanings" is from the perspective of a yogin, not from our own perspective, because we lack specific knowledge of all words and their respective meanings.

Furthermore, such knowledge in general is not conducive to true understanding. It must be understood that the scripture (*śāstra*) was indeed composed for the sake of people like us. In that regard, the creation of technical terminology (*saṅketa-śāstra*) by one's own will is what constitutes their status as "arbitrary words" (*yadṛcchā-śabda*); it is said that "names are created by one's own will. Prior to the acquisition of the status of a name through instruction in this form of convention, there is the conventional usage of those [words] as being non-eternal (*anitya*), because their status as names has not yet been grasped.

For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule defining the technical term *saṅkhyā*, it is stated that the restriction (*niyama*)—consisting in the non-apprehension of any other meaning—is rooted in the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), based on the context (*prakaraṇa*) which consists of the knowledge of the application of those respective technical names. By adopting this very implied restriction (*ārthika-niyama*), the designation of "restriction" (*niyamatva-vyavahāra*) is applied to the rules for technical names (*saṃjñā-sūtra*) in such passages as: "A restriction of a name [is made] for the sake of usage, [stating] that a name applies to a named object only in certain cases," and so forth. Even though these rules convey the denotative capacity (*vācakatā*) [of the name], there is no loss of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning (*śabdārtha-sambandha-nityatā*), because they do not actually produce that relationship.

The correctness (*sādhutva*) of these [forms] follows from their being employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*); this is explained in detail elsewhere. Even under the view that grammatical operations apply at the time of usage (*kāryakālapakṣa*), when there is a desire to know the meaning of the term *vṛddhi* in rules such as "vṛddhir eci" (P. 1.1.1), the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (P. 1.1.1) presents itself; once the apprehension of the power (*śaktigraha*)—which consists in the understanding of that meaning—has occurred, the understanding of the meaning of the prescriptive sentence (*vidhivākya*) follows. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (P. 6.1.13): "Under the view that technical terms and paribhāṣās apply at the time of usage, this [rule] 'bhasya' (P. 6.4.129) presents itself, and thus [the paribhāṣā] 'yaci bham' (P. 1.4.18) becomes applicable."

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *īdūded* [Pāṇini 1.1.11], it is stated: "When the time for application arrives, the technical rules (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) present themselves; thus, this [rule] 'the dual endings *ī*, *ū*, and *e* are *pragṛhya*' becomes applicable. Kaiyaṭa, too, on the sūtra *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 3.2.102], says: "When *niṣṭhā* is mentioned, the technical rule statement 'the suffix *ktavatu* is *niṣṭhā*' is recalled."

In this view (the *kāryakālapakṣa*), even when the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) has occurred in one location, there might be no comprehension of the meaning in another location because of the possibility that the power resides only in that specific place; therefore, the comprehension of the meaning of the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) must be preceded by the apprehension of the power of each respective word in every location. However, in the *yathoddeśapakṣa*, the distinction is that comprehension occurs everywhere at once due to the apprehension of the power occurring simultaneously. By this [it is shown that] in the *kāryakālapakṣa*, the use of the phoneme *t* as a marker (*taparatva*) is merely for the sake of clarity.

Since the referents of *āT*, *aiC*, and *auC* are prescribed as qualifiers for *vṛddhi*, there is no possibility of including their homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). The view that "wherever the word *vṛddhi* occurs, *āT-aiC* is supplied" [and thus] the meaning of the technical rule-sūtras (*saṃjñā-sūtra*) follows in sequence, is refuted; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Here, however, there is the inclusion of even those *āT*, *aiC*, and *auC* forms that have not undergone the [specific grammatical] transformation (*atadbhāvita*), by which the forms such as *śālīya* are established.

"Roots beginning with *bhū* [denote] actions. What is the purpose of specifying "denoting an action"? [Consider the case of] the particle *vā*, which expresses the sense of option (*vikalpa*). If it were a root, it would not be a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*); consequently, in the absence of a case-ending (*sub*), it would fail to attain the status of a word (*pada*). However, if it is stated that it denotes an action, there is no such fault. This is because the meaning of *vā*—namely, option—lacks connection with past or future time, and thus lacks the nature of an action (*kriyātva*). On the other hand, even the meaning of roots like *asti* (to be) possesses that nature because of its connection with past and future time. What is the purpose of specifying "beginning with *bhū*"? [The answer follows: [To exclude particles such as *ca* and *vā*, which do not denote actions.]

If *āṇavayati*, *vaṭṭayati*, and so forth were considered verbal roots (*dhātu*), they would result in grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) by virtue of falling within the scope of the grammatical treatise; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the remainder of the relevant Sūtra. As for *stambh* and the others, because they are marked with the *u*-diacritic (*udit*), they serve as the targets for operations prescribed under the heading of "verbal root" (*dhātu-adhikāra*); thus, there is no fault in them, as their current readings are inferred to have resulted from a corruption of the established text.

"Prior to *īśvara*": The governing rule (*adhikāra*) is that particles (*nipāta*) ending with "adhirīśvare" (Pāṇini 1.4.97) are [treated as such]. This means that those which are particles prior to that point are designated as *gati* and so forth. By this, their inclusion under those [designations]—such as in the rules "adhirīśvare" and "vibhāṣā kṛñi"—and their connection with the term "particle" (*nipāta*) are established. Whether these [particles] possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) or not is to be understood according to their specific function and usage; the details are explained elsewhere.

*su-p-tiṅ*. Regarding *sub*, the term *sup* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) formed by the letter *p*; this is established through traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). Although it might be argued that because of the rule "when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, that which ends with it is understood," the inclusion of that which ends in the suffix is established by taking the word-form itself as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), and that the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies because the suffix implies a collection (*samudāya*) of which its own base (*prakṛti*) is a constituent part, and thus serves as its qualifier—this is not correct. This is because in forms such as *iyān*, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from such a collection, making implication (*ākṣepa*) impossible; furthermore, what is merely implied cannot enter into a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) within the explicit expression of the sentence.

Nevertheless, in the rule for designating technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the mention of "end" (*anta*) is intended to indicate that when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix (*tadantagrahaṇa*). Consequently, the designation *gha* applies only to *taras* and *map*, not to that which ends in them. Thus, in the case of *gaurābrāhmaṇitarā*, the designation *hasta* does not apply. By the very force of this prohibition, there is likewise no application of the rule regarding the end of a word (*tadantavidhi*) in specific instances (*pradeśa*). And it should not be argued: "Even if this is indicated, [the mention of 'end'] is redundant; for in the case of words (*pada-pradeśa*), when a suffix is mentioned, the desired result is already established by the inclusion of what ends in that suffix. This is because [the present rule] serves as a restrictive indicator (*niyamaka*) even in the context of technical name designations. Otherwise, since the designation *gha* would apply to *taras* and *map* by the general rule of including what ends in them, the mention of "end" here would be useless. Therefore, it is understood that in the context of technical name designations, when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends in that suffix. This is why the designation *gha* does not apply to *gaurābrāhmaṇitarā*. Furthermore, it is not the case that the mention of "end" is redundant even in the context of words, because in that context, the inclusion of what ends in the suffix is established by the general rule of including what ends in that suffix. However, since the mention of "end" is necessary to prevent the designation *gha* from applying to *gaurābrāhmaṇitarā*, it is concluded that in the context of technical name designations, when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends in that suffix. Thus, the mention of "end" is not redundant. This is the meaning.

Since the status of being a *pada* (word) is common to both base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), when "word" (*pada*) is mentioned [in a rule], there is no mention of "suffix" at all. This is because of the continued application of the rule "from that which a suffix is prescribed" (*yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ*) and so forth; thus, a collection of words (*padasamudāya*) does not possess the status of a *pada*. In forms such as *iyān*, the fact that it begins with that from which a suffix is prescribed and ends with a *taddhita* suffix must be understood through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Therefore, even though the status of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) is not established by the technical rules of grammar, it is extended [to the whole] by this principle. The meaning of this is that operations caused by the linguistic usage residing in a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭaniṣṭa*) must be performed even for that which is not accompanied by a suffix (*asahāya*).

For this very reason, in examples such as *iyāmātram*, the suffix *mātraC* is established by the rule *vatvantāt svārthe*. However, in cases such as *hariṣu*, the suffix *su* does not function in this way as a word-final element (*padatva*), because the rule *hali sarveṣām* indicates that [the substitution] does not apply when [the suffix] is accompanied by another sound. This is stated in the Bhāṣya under the rule *nijau catvāra ekācaḥ* as an argument based on a specific admission (*abhyupetyavāda*). And this has been implied in the Bhāṣya under rules such as *ādeca upadeśe* and *tāsyanudāttata*.

For in that context, regarding the statement "tatra hi daukate," it was stated that the long vowel *au* in *aukārasya* and the short vowel *ā* in *hitāḥ*, etc., possess the status of being taught as having final vowels (*ajanta-upadeśatva*) or being taught as ending in the vowel *a* (*akārānta-upadeśatva*) by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing [the property of] the whole" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). This is for the sake of establishing meaningfulness (*arthavattā*). The meaning is this: the designation as if possessing [the property of the whole] applies to a phoneme (*varṇa*) that is itself meaningful. And the meaningfulness of a phoneme occurs only when it is not accompanied by another, as in examples such as *iyāya*; however, this is not the case in the present instance. Thus, the point is that the phrase "in one" (*ekasmin*) is expressed by the term "meaningful" (*arthavatā*). This is the general direction of the argument.

The term *anantarā* [is used] in the sense of "immediately following. In the case of "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred," just as the fine of one hundred applies to the group as a whole, so too the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to the group alone and not to each individual; this is because, given the statement "immediately following" (*anantarā*), it is more appropriate for that [term] to function as a qualifier of the group. As for what was said [in the *Saṃgraha*]: [...]*saṃ.* [Note: The provided text fragment ends here.]

The claim that "the term [saṃyoga] is an etymological designation (anvarthasaṃjñā) because phonemes (varṇāḥ) are joined (yujyante) therein, and thus it is not a designation for each individual [phoneme]" is incorrect. This is because in expressions such as *ghaṭapaṭau saṃyujyete* ("the jar and the cloth are joined"), there is a well-established linguistic usage (*vyutpannatva*) wherein the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is understood to be something distinct from the objects being joined; consequently, if this were the case, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) that the designation would apply to the entire collection consisting of those [phonemes] and the words containing them. The use of the grand designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*), however, is merely out of deference to the ancient grammarians (*prācām*).

Therefore, in the example *suhaṣaddhāti*, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) does not occur, as explained in detail elsewhere. The plural number in *halā* is a Vedic (sautra) usage.

Alternatively, there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) in the form "halau ca halaśca. This is established in the rule *svaritātsaṃhitāyām*, where the term *anudāttānām* involves such an *ekaśeṣa*. Even where many [consonants] are joined (*śliṣṭa*), it refers only to pairs and not to many, because the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga* is prescribed when an *ali* follows. The idea that it applies to many is indeed questionable, as there is no resulting benefit; for in each instance, the *saṃyoga* relied upon is specifically that which is part of an *aṅga*, a word, or a verbal root, and such a [conjunction] consists of only three [consonants].

“Immediacy” (*ānantarya*) means the absence of an intervention (*vyavadhāna*), and an intervention occurs only by means of a dissimilar element; thus he says: *ajbhir iti*. In this case, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*, *kh*, *g*, *gh*, *ṅ*) would be correct. For this very reason, the substitution of *ku* is seen in the Mādhyandina recension of the *Brāhmaṇa* in the passages “*iyannastabhūtra*” and “*aco’kṣu*”. The interpretation that [the consonants] are “not separated by vowels” (*svarair avyavahitāḥ*) is appropriate. Why [specify] “by consonants”? Consider *titau deva*. Here, by the rule “*guroḥ*” [Pāṇini 6.1.87], there would be a protracted vowel (*pluta*). Why [specify] “immediate” (*anantarāḥ*)? Consider *sam*. Here, because the *s* and *m* would constitute a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), the elision [of the *m*] by the rule “*ka*” [Pāṇini 8.2.23] would occur.

In rules such as *saṃyoga-gurū ‘bhettā*, the substitution of *guṇa* is to be understood by virtue of the fact that the suffix *kn* is treated as having the force of *kit*, and because of the inclusion of the term "having had a light penultimate vowel" (*bhūtapūrva-laghu-upadhā-grahaṇāt*). Thus ends [the section on] *san*. The meaning is that the section on technical designations (*saṃjñā*) useful for the operations of euphonic combination (*sandhi*) located in the first chapter is completed. Therefore, there is no deficiency even if the designations of *adaṇḍita-pragṛhya*, *asañjñā-lopa*, and *sañjñā-yaṇ* have not been introduced here; the introduction of "a a" and so forth was merely incidental. Thus ends the section on technical designations.
